selected_prs.title: fix(ai): keep usage and timing on thinking-loop aborts
selected_prs.body:
## What

I made a turn that omp stops for a thinking loop keep the usage, timing and response id the provider had already reported, because those turns were saved as free, instant requests stamped with the time they failed.

The loop guard replaces an aborted attempt with its own error message, and that message started from zeros. It now carries what the attempt that tripped had:

| Field on the saved error turn | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `usage` (tokens, cost) | all 0 | what the provider had reported when the guard tripped |
| `responseId` | missing | the provider's id (OpenRouter's is the generation id) |
| `duration`, `ttft` | missing | from that attempt's start to the trip and to its first delta |
| `timestamp` | when it failed | when the attempt started, like every other turn |

## Why

Thinking-loop aborts are long turns: 5 aborted DeepSeek V4.1 Flash turns on OpenRouter in my sessions had each streamed 10–23 s against ~116k tokens of context, and all 7 saved loop aborts in my transcripts read $0 with no duration.

How much usage there is depends on the wire. Providers that report usage while streaming (Anthropic at `message_start`, Gemini on every chunk) hand it over; Responses and Chat Completions report it only at the end, so those turns still read 0 tokens but now keep the response id, which on OpenRouter is enough to look the generation's real cost up.

Decisions:
- Timing is tied to the provider snapshot the guard last saw: a provider retry starts a new snapshot, so its backoff and the earlier attempt never count. The guard does not wait for the aborted provider to finish, which would put its teardown on the retry path.
- A loop found at the end-of-stream flush takes the final message, timing included.
- Leaked-thinking healing (non-official endpoints) projected a copy of the provider's message made at stream start, so usage a provider replaces later (Gemini does per chunk) never reached the guard; the projection now follows the source's non-content fields.

Non-goals: estimating unreported tokens from the streamed text. Session totals (`getSessionStats`) count only messages still in context, and a retried error turn leaves context, so the recovered attempt's usage shows in the session journal but not there; that holds for every retried error kind and is separate.

## Testing

Through the real providers (`stream()` with a scripted SSE response that repeats one sentence until the guard trips):

| Wire | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic, `claude-haiku-4-5` | 0 tokens, $0, no id, no timing | 116,000 input, $0.116, `msg_loop`, ttft and duration set |
| OpenRouter Responses, `deepseek-v4.1-flash` | 0 tokens, no id, no timing | 0 tokens (none reported yet), `gen-loop-1`, ttft and duration set |

Four new cases in `thinking-loop.test.ts` (usage, start, id and timing kept; a retried attempt reports only itself; the end-of-stream flush takes the final message; usage replaced mid-stream reaches the guard through leaked-thinking healing) fail with the source changes reverted; the last fails with only the healing change reverted. The ai suite passes (6,058).

```
bun test packages/ai/test/thinking-loop.test.ts
```

selected_prs.body:
Runs started by pi.sendMessage(..., { triggerTurn: true }) skipped before_agent_start. After their first tool call, the next-turn refresh fell back to the base prompt options and patched away the sections handlers had added, changing the system prompt mid-run and breaking the provider prompt cache.

The session counts as busy from the start of setup, so messages sent while handlers run go into the starting run instead of starting a second one, and an abort requested meanwhile aborts the run once it starts.

selected_prs.title: fix(coding-agent): resolve model references through one provider selection policy
selected_prs.body:
Fixes #10160

## Problem

When the named provider lacks a model but several gateways expose `provider/id` as a raw id, `--model provider/id` picked the first gateway in catalog order, ignoring credentials:

```text
pi --model anthropic/claude-opus-5.5   # only vercel-ai-gateway has a key
-> openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 (listed first)
```

Provider selection was spread across branches that discarded ambiguity, so results also depended on input shape: `shared` picked the authenticated provider, `shared:high` picked by catalog order.

## Change

`resolveModelReference` in `core/model-resolver.ts` resolves every model reference (`--model`, `--models`/`enabledModels`, `/model`, `pi auth print-*`) in one pipeline. It collects all candidates, then applies one rule: the named provider's match if usable, else the sole usable raw match, else the named provider's match, else ambiguous. Fuzzy matching runs only when no reference candidate exists and prefers usable providers.

## Behavior changes

- No unique authenticated provider among exact matches is now an error, not catalog order.
- Fuzzy matches prefer authenticated providers; an identical best id on several providers is ambiguous.
- With `--api-key`, stored credentials no longer pick the provider.
- `--models`/`enabledModels` patterns add every provider offering the same id and warn about the ambiguity.

`provider/id` still prefers the named provider's exact or fuzzy match.

selected_prs.title: feat(durable): support namespaced SQLite storage
selected_prs.body:
## Summary

Some use cases may require Pi Durable to share a single SQLite database, e.g. Cloudflare Durable Object could store additional data, unrelated to the harness in other tables. To isolate Pi Durable storage from the rest, this PR introduces the option to provide a table prefix. A prefix `pi_` results in table names like `pi_conversations` instead of `conversations` for instance, same for index names.

- add optional SQLite table and index prefixes rendered from one portable schema map
- expose prefixing through `SqliteStorage.open()`, `openNodeSqliteStorage()`, and `openDurableObjectSqliteStorage()` helper
- keep adapters prefix-agnostic by rendering names in storage SQL; split Node database options from combined Node storage options
- validate Node prefixes before creating or configuring the database
- simplify the Cloudflare adapter by removing SQL rewriting while improving cursor reads and cross-adapter transaction ordering
- document prefix behaviour and cover host-table coexistence plus multiple isolated namespaces

Changing a prefix does not migrate existing data.

## Testing

- `npm run check`
- `vitest --run test/sqlite-cloudflare.test.ts test/sqlite-migrations.test.ts test/sqlite-facade.test.ts test/sqlite-storage.test.ts` (111 tests)

selected_prs.title: Restore ACP sessions after unexpected agent exits
selected_prs.body:
🚨 **SLOP COP** 🚨 · `new-issue-autopilot`

## Root cause
When an established ACP agent exited, the bridge deleted the saved state it needs to rebuild the session. Rejected prompts also cleared the active-prompt marker before the asynchronous exit callback could emit a failed completion, so the runtime turn stayed active.

## Change
- Keep established sessions that exited unexpectedly. The next turn reuses the existing resume/rebuild path: agents that support `session/load` keep the provider session ID. If loading is unsupported or fails, the existing explicit context-loss fallback applies.
- Fail an interrupted turn as soon as its prompt is rejected because the agent connection dropped. Do not wait for process-tree cleanup to finish. The exit callback still sends the thread-level warning. Without this, a steer sent during cleanup (up to about 2s when the agent leaves descendants behind) was accepted and then replayed into the next turn, and a new turn was refused with "A turn is already active".
- Dynamic tool calls still reject dead connections. Explicit stops, releases, stale callbacks, and failed construction still remove sessions.
- Merged `main` to pick up the unpublished plugin SDK 0.6.20 bump. The bundled ACP bridge changed, so the npm version guard needs it.

Fixes #4939

Report: https://get-bb.github.io/reports/issues/4939.html

## Verification
- All 8 focused exit/recovery tests fail against the base bridge (`ef570298ef`) and pass with this change, 3/3 runs. They cover clean and nonzero exits, idle and active turns, successful/unsupported/failed `session/load`, and a steer plus new turn sent while the exited agent's process tree is still being cleaned up.
- The cleanup-window test fails on the PR's first commit (`c61737b4bd`): the interrupted turn only failed after the agent's leftover child process had been killed. The test orders on the bridge's own failed-turn event and runs on POSIX only, because the cleanup window comes from process-group termination; Windows tree termination removes the descendant immediately. A probe on that commit showed the bug end to end: the follow-up `turn/start` returned "A turn is already active", and the stale steer was later sent to the agent after the next prompt.
- Exit-message assertions no longer depend on exit code 0, which Windows does not produce for an external kill. The single-exit test now waits for the second completion instead of reading the last existing one, which was racy.
- `turbo run lint typecheck` passes for `@bb/provider-bridge-acp` and `@bb/agent-runtime`. Full suites pass: ACP bridge 374 passed / 4 skipped, agent runtime 307 passed.
- No dependency, generated-file, stored-data, or host/daemon protocol change.

selected_prs.title: Honor machine selection for personal child environments
selected_prs.body:
🚨 **SLOP COP** 🚨 · `new-issue-autopilot`

## Human comments

## What was wrong

The Personal-project child policy replaced personal workspace requests with the parent's environment before checking the selected machine. A different existing host or a new-machine selection was silently discarded. The [verified reproduction report](https://get-bb.github.io/reports/issues/5204.html) records failures on trusted main in two clean checkouts.

## What changed

- Reuse the parent's personal environment only when machine selection is omitted or selects the parent's existing host.
- Preserve different-host and new-machine requests for the existing environment placement implementation.
- Extend the existing policy test table with a real stored parent environment and matching-host, different-host, omitted-machine, and new-machine cases.
- Two files in the existing server thread-policy subsystem; 95 changed text lines (87 additions, 8 deletions). No dependencies, generated files, data changes, public contracts, wire fields, or CLI flags change.

selected_prs.title: Make the rebuilt ACP adapter the only ACP adapter
selected_prs.body:
## Human comments

## What was wrong

bb shipped two ACP adapters side by side: the original (`packages/provider-bridge-acp`, plugin `provider-acp`, on by default) and the rebuilt one from #5266 (`packages/provider-bridge-acp-next`, plugin `bb--provider-acp-next`, opt-in and mutually exclusive through `BUNDLED_PLUGIN_REPLACEMENTS`). Fixes had to be made twice, and some weren't: #5374's shutdown cleanup only reached the original bridge. Deleting the original plugin directly would have caused data loss. The orphaned-builtin cleanup (`removeUnbundledBuiltins`) deletes a removed built-in's settings, so every default user's `customAgents` would have been wiped. Users who had opted in would have been left with `provider-acp` disabled and no ACP providers.

## What changed

- **In-place swap.** The rebuilt bridge and plugin now live at `packages/provider-bridge-acp` and `plugins/provider-acp`, under the original package names and the `provider-acp` plugin id. Default users' plugin rows, `customAgents`, and threads carry over unchanged, since provider ids are the same (`acp-cursor`, …). The `-next` directories are deleted. So are the opt-in switch (`BUNDLED_PLUGIN_REPLACEMENTS`, the `standsAside` catalog filter and the paired enable/disable in `setEnabled`) and their tests. Hardcoded `bb--provider-acp-next` ids in the plugin (`known-agents.ts`, `registry-icons.ts`, `usage-source.ts`) are now `provider-acp`. Registry icon refs resolve as `provider-acp/registry-*`.
- **Handover for opted-in users.** `RETIRED_BUNDLED_PLUGINS` in `builtin-registry.ts` declares `bb--provider-acp-next` → `provider-acp`. At startup, `handOverRetiredBuiltins()` runs before `removeUnbundledBuiltins()`. If the retired row was enabled, it copies `customAgents` to `provider-acp` and turns `provider-acp` on. Then it deletes the retired row's settings, secrets and schedules. It does not clear the user's disabled-provider list, which normal orphan cleanup would, because both plugins own the same provider ids.
- **Plugin SDK.** `@get-bb/plugin-sdk/provider-bridge/acp` now exports the rebuilt bridge. The export names and type shapes are the same as before, plus `experimental_registerAcpDialect`. `provider-bridge/acp-next` stays as a deprecated alias re-exporting `/acp`. `docs/api_to_audit.md` merges the two entries. No wire change; `HostDaemonAcpLaunchSpec` is identical.
- **#5374 ported to the rebuilt bridge.** Every agent connection (thread sessions, model discovery, session-option discovery) is tracked and removed on exit. New connections are refused once shutdown starts. stdin close, SIGTERM and SIGINT share one awaited cleanup that releases sessions and kills tracked agents. Includes `shutdown.test.ts` from #5374.
- **References.** Updated `bundled-plugins`, `bb-official.json`, `first-party-plugins.json`, `forkable-plugins.json`, the web bundled-marketplace list, `turbo.json` (the -next task config moved to `bb-plugin-provider-acp`), the provider-literal ratchet, plugin-build tests, `docs/configuration.md`, and the bb-guide plugin-authoring references.

## How you verified

- `pnpm exec turbo run typecheck lint` for `@bb/provider-bridge-acp`, `bb-plugin-provider-acp`, `@get-bb/plugin-sdk`, `@bb/server`, `@bb/web`, `@bb/domain`, and `@bb/plugin-build`. All passed.
- `turbo run test` passed for the bridge (505 tests, including the 6 ported shutdown cases), the SDK (376), plugin-build (211) and domain (248).
  - The plugin package had 81 of 82 passing. The one failure is `native-roots.test.ts` omp, an environment-only failure because `/tmp/.agents` exists on the machine (per `.bb/skills/test-audit`). It passes with `TMPDIR=/var/tmp/...`.
- Server: `vitest run` over `test/services/plugins`, `test/services/plugin-catalog`, `test/system/provider-management`, `test/system/execution-options`, `test/public/public-provider-installations` and `test/providers/provider-registry`: 65 files and 765 tests passed. That includes the new `retired-bundled-plugins.test.ts`, which covers three cases: an enabled retired plugin hands off settings and turns its successor on; a disabled one leaves the successor alone and keeps disabled providers; and a missing successor.
- `packages/agent-runtime` `runtime.acp-topology.test.ts` passed.
- `node scripts/check-plugin-forks.mjs plugins/provider-acp` passed (with a clean TMPDIR). The provider-literal ratchet passed. The plugin SDK npm version guard passed (0.6.56 is unpublished, so no bump).

selected_prs.title: fix(acp): cancel running turns before killing agents on shutdown
selected_prs.body:
## Human comments

## What was wrong

When bb shut a provider worker down (stdin close, SIGTERM or SIGINT), the ACP bridge released every session and killed every agent at once. ACP agents run their tool commands in process groups of their own, so a command running at that moment outlived bb, re-parented to init. A normal `thread stop` doesn't leave them, because it sends `session/cancel` first and the agent ends its own commands. #5374 added the shutdown hooks but deliberately skipped the cancel, to stay inside the runtime's 5 s escalation window.

Found while live-testing #5775: Ctrl-C of bb mid-turn left Cursor's and OpenCode's `sleep 120` running under systemd.

## What changed

- `packages/provider-bridge-acp/src/bridge/bridge.ts`: shutdown stops each session through `stopSession` with a 1.5 s cancel window (`SHUTDOWN_CANCEL_TIMEOUT_MS`). All sessions are stopped in parallel, so total shutdown stays well inside 5 s. Connections owned by no session (model/option discovery, sessions still starting) are killed straight away, and anything left is killed afterwards. Previously one `allSettled` killed every connection in parallel with releasing sessions, so the agent died before it could handle a cancel.
- `shutdown.test.ts`: new case per shutdown path. A fake agent starts a detached child on `session/prompt` and kills it on `session/cancel`; the test asserts the child is gone once the bridge exits.

## How you verified

- The three new cases (SIGTERM, SIGINT, stdin) fail before the change with "the agent's command outlived the bridge". They pass after it, as do the six existing reap cases.
- `pnpm exec turbo run test lint typecheck --filter=@bb/provider-bridge-acp`: 508 passed, 4 skipped.
- Live, on an isolated `start:worktree` build with real cursor-agent 2026.08.11 and opencode 1.18.35: both threads ran `sleep 120`, then bb got Ctrl-C (SIGINT to its process group). Before the fix, both sleeps survived. After it, ports are free and no `sleep`, `cursor-agent acp` or `opencode acp` process is left.

selected_prs.title: fix(acp): enforce bb permission modes for OpenCode
selected_prs.body:
## Human comments

## What was wrong

bb passed OpenCode no permission policy, so OpenCode's own config decided. With the default config, OpenCode ran shell commands without asking even when the thread was in `accept-edits`, while Cursor asked for the same commands. Found while live-testing #5775.

## What changed

- The bridge launches OpenCode-dialect agents with `OPENCODE_PERMISSION`, which OpenCode merges over the `permission` keys of its config:
  - **`accept-edits`:** `edit` is allowed; `bash`, `webfetch` and `external_directory` ask. OpenCode's ACP permission requests become bb approvals.
  - **`full`:** all four are allowed.
- A permission-mode change restarts the OpenCode session with the new policy, and OpenCode restores the conversation. Permission CLI flags already work this way for other agents.
- Other dialects get no OpenCode policy.
- `dialectLaunchEnv` now also holds the existing `OPENCODE_CLIENT` / `OPENCODE_ENABLE_QUESTION_TOOL` values.
- The acp-provider skill documents the behaviour.

## How you verified

- New bridge tests:
  - an OpenCode session gets the `full` policy, then the `accept-edits` policy after a mode change, and the session is replaced with `contextLost: false`;

selected_prs.title: feat(orchestration): a native chat can be a dispatch worker, like a terminal agent
selected_prs.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 14 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1089 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​27 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1062 |
| Prod | 40 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​929 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​145 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​784 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## The problem

Orca's orchestration lets one agent (the coordinator) hand a task to another agent (a worker), follow its progress, and collect its result. A worker could be an agent running in a terminal pane, or a native-chat worker that Orca started itself, but not a native chat that already exists (Orca's built-in chat view for Claude and Codex). Asking for one was refused. `dispatch --to orca_session_id:<id>` answered `session_chat_not_dispatchable` ("a chat can't receive a dispatch yet"), and `worker-start --terminal orca_session_id:<id>` failed with a misleading `terminal_handle_stale`. So a coordinator could not hand work to a chat that already had the right context; it had to start a fresh worker instead.

## ELI5

Any native chat can now be given a task the way a terminal agent is. The coordinator uses the same two commands and names the chat by the ID every chat agent is already shown (`orca_session_id:<id>`) instead of a terminal handle. The chat gets the task the way a message you type gets there: if it is idle, the task starts a turn; if it is busy, the task waits in the chat's queue as a normal card, which you can see, pause or delete like your own. The task is labelled with who sent it ("Message from <coordinator>", and "From <coordinator>" on a waiting card), like other agents' messages in a chat. The chat reports back with the same `worker_done` command a terminal worker uses, and the coordinator lists, shows, reads, stops and abandons it with the same commands. Stopping or abandoning it never closes your chat.

## What this changes for you

| Situation | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| A coordinator gives an existing chat a task (`dispatch --to orca_session_id:<id> --inject`, or `worker-start --terminal orca_session_id:<id>`) | Refused | Accepted. The chat gets the task and reports with `worker_done`, like a terminal worker |
| The chat is idle | — | The task starts a turn at once. `worker-start` answers `ready` |
| The chat is busy with your own turn | — | Your turn finishes untouched. The task waits as a card in the chat's queue and is sent as its own turn after yours. `worker-start` answers `outcome_unknown` and says the task is waiting as a queued card, the same answer a terminal start gives when it can't see the agent begin |
| You press Stop, or Orca restarts, while the task card waits | — | The card is paused, like your own queued messages, until you send a message or press Resume. You can also delete it |
| `worker-list` / `worker-show` on the chat worker | — | `live` while the chat is open (also when it is resting and its next message would start it), `exited` once you close it, `unverifiable` when this machine can't tell (for example, a chat on another host) |
| `worker-read` | — | Reads the chat's current conversation, following `/clear` |
| `worker-stop` / `worker-abandon` | — | The task is stopped or abandoned; your chat stays open and keeps whatever it is doing, as a terminal reused with `--terminal` does |
| You close the chat while it has a task | — | The task fails as "closed by operator", the same as closing a terminal worker's pane |
| Mail the coordinator sends to the worker (`dispatch:<id>`) | — | Reaches the chat's "you have new messages" notice, as for a terminal worker |
| A chat on another machine (SSH, WSL, a paired host) | — | Refused with the existing host-boundary error, as mail to it is |

## What Changed

- **The task goes through the chat's own send.** It uses `sendAgentTurn` with queueing on, exactly like the "you have new messages" notice and like a message you send with queueing on. There is no separate task store, hold, retry or readiness gate. The message records who it is from (`body.from`) with a new `task` kind: the sender, Run, task and Dispatch. The chat then names the coordinator the way it names any agent's message. A native-chat worker that Orca starts itself gets the same label on its task.
- **One send per Dispatch.** The send's operation ID is derived from the Dispatch, so a retried request replays the first answer instead of queueing the task twice.
- **`worker-start` reads the send's outcome with existing states only.** Accepted means `ready`. Queued or not yet started means `outcome_unknown`; the task has been handed over and is not resent. Refused or rejected means `failed`. A chat's Dispatch records the chat by its Orca session ID (the ID it had before any `/clear`) and has no pane or process, so a chat worker's own sub-dispatches count toward the nesting limit.
- **Liveness is read from the chat's records**, the same rule the mail lane uses to decide whether a chat can be reached. Only a chat you closed reads `exited`; missing evidence reads `unverifiable`, never `exited`.
- **Closing a chat settles its Dispatch** through the same path a closed terminal pane uses, once the close is proven. A close that is rolled back (for example a worktree delete Orca refuses) leaves the task alone.
- **Refusals.** These cover an unknown chat, a provider's own session ID, a chat on another host, a closed chat, a chat in a different worktree than the worker, and a chat handing a task to itself with `--inject`; each is refused before anything is created. A chat that already has an active task is refused too. `dispatch` refuses it up front; `worker-start` fails it the same way it fails a terminal that already has one, after recording the new task as failed. `worker-start --on <host> --terminal orca_session_id:` is refused at home, before any remote call.
- **`dispatch --inject` to a chat keeps the connection alive** while the chat's agent starts. A chat at rest can take longer than the socket's idle limit to accept, which used to read as "Restart Orca". Only chat targets get this; terminal `--inject` is unchanged.
- **Coordinator mail that was held when the chat's agent stopped is pointed at again** on the chat's next idle moment, including in the session a `/clear` continued it in, as for a terminal worker.
- **The command name in the task text** for any native-chat worker is the one its mail notices use (`orca-dev` in a dev build), instead of always `orca`.

## Why

Before this change, a chat could not be a worker at all. An earlier version of this PR gave the task its own store, its own delivery lane and a readiness check, and live testing showed what that costs: a second "is the chat free?" rule beside the queue's own drifted from it, and a task could be merged into a turn the user had just started. Sending the task through the chat's existing send and queue removes that class of bug, because there is only one rule. It is also the common pattern for one agent messaging another: the message uses the same send a person's does, and the queued row records who sent it.

Where a terminal worker lives with an edge, the chat lives with the same one instead of gaining an extra rule.

## Differences from a terminal worker

- **Intended: a busy chat queues the task instead of making `worker-start` wait for it to go idle.** The queue already protects your turn, and the task card is visible and deletable.
- **Intended: stopping or abandoning a task does not withdraw a task card that is still waiting.** It is your card to keep or delete. If it later runs, the chat's `worker_done` for the ended task is refused. A terminal handed a task with `--inject` while busy behaves the same way.
- **Intended: deleting a waiting task card leaves the task open** until the coordinator abandons it. The coordinator gets no signal, as when you clear input typed into a terminal worker. A deletion is your action, and it never settles orchestration bookkeeping for you.
- **Intended: after an Orca restart, a waiting task card stays paused until you act.** This matches your own queued messages and mail notices. A terminal's own input queue would send it.
- **Intended: a chat on another host is refused,** as mail to it is, until reach to it can be proven.
- **Temporary: a coordinator on a paired remote client keeps its own 60-second timeout** without keepalives. A very slow chat start can read as a timeout there even though the task was delivered. `terminal.send` with an agent prompt has the same gap today.

## Compatibility

- **Mixed versions.** The sender travels on the message to clients, like any agent message. An older client or host that doesn't know the `task` kind keeps the sender and drops only the task details, so it still shows "From <coordinator>", and opening the sender looks it up by its address. The one removed error code, `session_chat_not_dispatchable`, has no remaining reader.
- **SSH / WSL / remote.** A chat whose session runs on another host is refused. Loss of contact never reads as `exited`.

Part of the native-chat orchestration work (no separate issue).

## Testing

- They cover:
  - an idle chat taking its task;
  - a busy chat holding it as one card;
  - a retry queueing nothing new;
  - self-dispatch, other-host, wrong-worktree and remote `--on` refusals;
  - the coordinator's mail reaching the chat;
  - the nesting limit;
  - stop and abandon leaving the chat open;
  - a closed chat failing its Dispatch, and a rolled-back close not failing it;
  - a `/clear` successor reporting as the chat;
  - the chat's `worker_done` admitted and two forged senders refused;
  - the downgrade decode.
- Each key behaviour's test was checked to fail with its production line reverted.
- New tests also cover the sender on the task and on a native-chat worker Orca starts, held coordinator mail pointed at again after a `/clear`, and opening a task's sender.
- On the final head, targeted suites pass locally (the chat, mail, sender, `/clear` and close suites). The node, CLI and web typechecks pass, and oxlint is clean. CI is green.

selected_prs.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 17 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​491 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​509 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​18 |
| Prod | 17 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​611 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​119 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​492 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## The problem

When an agent sends orchestration mail to an agent that runs as a native chat (a structured session), the chat did not get it the way a CLI agent does.

The code that tells an agent about new mail had its own path for chats: its own rules for when a chat counts as busy (a turn running, or a question waiting for you), and its own send, outside the chat's send button and queue.

While the chat was busy, you saw nothing. Orca held the notice back and sent it later, by itself, when its own rules said the chat was free.

So a chat behaved differently from a CLI agent and from your own messages, and there was a second set of "is it busy?" rules to keep in step with the chat's own.

## What this changes for you

A native chat now gets exactly the line a CLI agent gets: "You have N orchestration messages. Run `orca orchestration check`." It comes through the same send as the messages you type, and the chat's queue gives it no special handling: it is held, sent, paused and resumed exactly like a message you queue.

| | Before | After |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mail arrives while the chat is idle | The notice is sent as a turn by Orca's own send | The notice is sent as a turn at once, through the chat's own send |
| Mail arrives while the chat is busy | Nothing is shown; Orca holds the notice and sends it later on its own | The notice waits above the composer as a normal queued card (Steer, Delete), and is sent when the turn ends |
| More mail arrives before the agent has read the mail it was told about | Held with the rest | It gets its own notice, counting only the mail not yet announced, as a terminal agent does. While the chat is busy, that is a second queued card |
| You press Stop | The notice is held by Orca's own rules, out of sight | The card waits under "Queue paused because you interrupted", with Resume, like your own cards |
| Orca restarts with a notice card waiting | (no card existed) | The card is held by the restart pause, with Resume, like your own cards |
| You delete a notice card | (no card existed) | Nothing is sent in its place. Its mail stays unread, and `check` still returns it. Later mail gets its own notice |
| The agent runs `orca orchestration check` | Returns its unread mail | Unchanged |

Agents running in a terminal are unchanged.

## How it works

The code that tells a chat about new mail sends the same text the terminal path types (`formatMessagePointer`, with the same command name) through `sendAgentTurn`, the one function for agent-to-agent sends, with delivery `queue`. That is the composer's own "queue if the chat is busy" send: an idle chat starts the turn, a busy chat's queue holds it as a card. The orchestration code does not know or check which happened, and it never reads, watches or waits on the chat's queue. The separate "is the chat busy?" rules for this path are deleted.

Agent notices get no special handling in the native-chat queue. The queue code is the same as on `main` apart from storing one column (below); nothing in it looks at who a card is from.

Which mail a notice counts uses the terminal path's rule unchanged. When a notice is sent or queued, its mail is marked as announced (the existing `delivered_at` marking that keeps the same mail from being announced twice), so the next notice counts only newer mail. The existing rule that no notice goes out while a `check` batch is waiting to be acknowledged is unchanged.

`check`, and which mail counts as read, are exactly as before: only `check` reads mail.

Each card records who it is from in `queued_messages.source_json`: the senders, and the messages it points at. This is for the next PR, which shows the sender on the card. It is data only: it changes no behaviour, it is stored on this machine only, never sent to any client, and a client's own send cannot set it. /clear carries it with the card.

## Why this approach

Brennan's direction: a native chat should behave exactly like a CLI agent for orchestration, reusing the send the chat already has, with no special handling for agent messages in the chat's queue, and without waiting for the chat to be idle.

Earlier versions of this PR sent the mail itself as the turn, then tracked what each card carried and let agent cards skip the restart pause. That needed rules to hide, withdraw and re-check queued cards. Sending the CLI agent's notice through the chat's own queue removes all of that. A later version also held back a second notice while earlier announced mail was unread; Brennan asked to keep that the same as CLI agents for now, so it is removed.

## What you might notice

The label says whether it stays (intended) or a follow-up removes it (temporary).

- Several messages during one busy turn can queue several cards, each "You have 1 orchestration message". A terminal agent instead gets one notice at its next idle moment for all new mail. The first card's `check` returns everything unread, so a later card's `check` may find nothing new. Intended: Orca does not wait for the chat to be idle, and a queued card is never rewritten.
- After a restart or a Stop, a waiting notice card needs Resume, like your own cards. Intended: the queue treats every card the same.
- If the agent's last turn failed to start in a way Orca cannot confirm, a new notice waits as a card until that clears, just as a message you send then would. Intended: it is the chat's own send rule.
- Mail that arrives after the agent ran `check` but did not acknowledge that batch (`--ack`) is not pointed until it does. Intended: unchanged from before, and the same for terminal agents.
- In this build, queueing your own messages is not switched on for chats, so a message you type while the agent works goes straight into the running turn, while the agent's notice waits as a card. Temporary: it lines up once your messages queue too, which is a separate setting this PR does not change.
- The notice appears in the conversation as a right-hand bubble, like a message you sent. Temporary: the next PR labels it with its sender.

## Differences from the common pattern

- The common pattern steers an agent's message into a busy chat; this PR queues it until the turn ends. Intended: Brennan asked for the composer's queue, which already exists so that a turn is not interrupted.
- The common pattern delivers an agent's message as the turn's text; this PR sends a notice, and the agent reads the mail with `check`. Intended: it is exactly what CLI agents get, and the mailbox stays the single record of what was read.

## Linked Issue

N/A: maintainer change, no issue.

## Visual Proof

From the live run on an earlier version of this PR (see Testing). These four states are unchanged by the later simplification.

Busy chat: the notice waits as a normal card while the turn runs.

![v3-s1-card-midturn.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/40670173-65ce-4551-8d70-357a35ac6521)

The turn ends, the notice is sent once, and the agent runs `check`.

![v3-s1-after-pointer-and-check.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/52bbcfa3-2617-47ba-8592-49bc17bc47df)

Idle chat: the notice is sent at once and the agent runs `check`.

![v3-s2-idle-pointer-turn.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/472ab208-47f0-4b9a-8532-03838f9a74a1)

After Stop: the card waits under "Queue paused because you interrupted", with Resume.

![v3-s6-after-stop.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/972c1385-628f-4d7c-a31e-cd62fa4f143e)

## Testing

Automated tests. Each behaviour test below, except the second-card test (new on this head), was checked by removing the code it covers and watching it fail.
- An idle chat gets the notice at once, the same bytes a terminal agent is typed (real host).
- A busy chat queues it as a card, with its sender stored, and sends it once when the turn ends (real host).
- Mail that arrives while an earlier notice waits gets its own card, counting only the new mail; each is sent in turn (unit, and end to end on the real host).
- /clear carries a card's sender with it; a card from before the column reads as the person's.
- Stop and restart: the existing queue suites (changed only to pass the new column), since agent cards take no other path.
- `check` is unchanged for a chat (the mail stays readable and the card stays) and for terminals (the existing suites, unmodified).

The orchestration and orchestration-messaging test directories and the native-chat queue suites pass. `pnpm tc:node` and `pnpm tc:cli` pass on this head.

Live run on macOS against a real Claude chat, at 8f2904d, an earlier version of this PR. Rows marked "changed since" no longer describe this head and were not re-run:

| Case | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| Idle chat gets the notice at once | Pass |
| Busy chat: one card, sent once at turn end, then the agent ran `check` | Pass |
| Three messages in one busy turn: one card | Pass; then one extra notice whose check found nothing new. Changed since: each message that arrives while the turn runs now queues its own card |
| Delete the card: not sent later, `check` still returns the mail | Pass |
| Stop holds the card with Resume; Resume sends it | Pass |
| Restart with only an agent card waiting: sent without Resume | Changed since: the restart pause now holds it, with Resume, like your cards |

Platforms: macOS. Linux, Windows and SSH share this code path; nothing here is platform-specific, and remote chats are not reached by this delivery.

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |

| Test | 30 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1774 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​89 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1685 |
| Prod | 86 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​2114 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​968 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1146 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

A phone paired with a desktop now shows the workspaces on the Orca servers that desktop is connected to,
not just the desktop's own and SSH workspaces. You can open them and use them from the phone, and every
request goes through the desktop. Each server's badge shows its health, for example "Update needed" or
"Disconnected", the same way the desktop does.

**Base: `main`.** The desktop's server list (#26442) and the e2e harness (#26412) have both merged, so
this diff is only this PR.

**Stack and merge order.**
1. #26501 (server workspaces on the phone) merges first.
2. Then #26519, #26521, #26533 and #26518, each stacked on #26501.
3. Then #27728 (needs #26519 and #26533) and #27749 (needs #26501).
4. Then #27741 (needs #27728).

Phones need the new native app release before server workspaces open. Until then, opening one shows
the existing screen "Your phone can't reach this workspace's server through this desktop."

## What Changed

**Before:** a phone paired with a desktop never showed workspaces from the remote Orca servers that desktop
connects to.

**After:**
- **Listing.** The phone lists every server workspace the desktop shows, fetched through the desktop
  (`mobileRelay.hosts.list` / `.worktrees`).
  - The host badge adds the server's health using the desktop's labels.
  - While a server can't be reached, the desktop keeps serving its last rows and the phone keeps showing
    them under that server's health badge. A server the desktop stops listing
    loses its rows.
  - The phone shows exactly the hosts the desktop's sidebar shows (`visibleWorkspaceHostIds`).
- **One shared server-list feed.** The host list and every open server workspace read the desktop's
  server list from one feed per desktop connection (`relay-hosts-feed.ts`), polled every 3 seconds only
  while something is reading it and the app is in the foreground. The next read is scheduled from when
  the last one finished, so a slow reply can't stop the polling. A reply from before a disconnect is
  thrown away, so an old answer never lands on a new connection.
- **A server workspace's connection state.** A server workspace no longer borrows the desktop's
  green dot. It reads:
  - **connected** only when the desktop can relay to that server now;
  - **connecting** while the desktop is reconnecting to the server, or has reached it but is still waiting
    for its status, matching the desktop's reconnecting banner;
  - **disconnected** when the server is too old to relay to, the desktop reports it failed, or it is no
    longer listed.

  It reuses the phone's existing connecting and disconnected screens, and reloads the tabs when the
  server comes back. Before this, a stopped server kept a green dot and "Loading tabs" spun forever.
- **Using a server workspace.** Every screen in a server workspace sends its calls to that server through
  the desktop: terminal, files, source control, diff, preview and agent history.
  - The target is set once, at the workspace route (`WorkspaceRoute` / `useWorkspaceClient`), so screens
    never choose one themselves.
  - Feature gates read the server's own `status.get`, not the desktop's.
  - Pinning a server workspace writes to that server.
- **Old servers and unreachable servers.**
  - Tapping a row on a server that needs an update shows the existing notice banner: "Update Orca on
    <host> to open its workspaces from your phone."
  - If the phone can't reach a server through this desktop (an older app or desktop, or an unreadable
    status), the workspace shows the existing "unavailable" screen with "Your phone can't reach this
    workspace's server through this desktop." The phone never quietly falls back to the desktop.
- **Wire.**
  - The phone names the server with an `executionHost` field. It travels in the general-purpose
    request envelope from #27815, which every transport (direct, cloud relay, shell bridge) already
    copies onto the wire request, including stream replays and unsubscribes. On the wire the field
    still sits at the top level of the request, as before.
  - Server rows appear only when the phone can actually reach them: the desktop advertises the relay
    capability AND the transport carries an envelope. The native app always does. A page does only
    when its shell grants `rpcEnvelope`. Under an older app, the page shows exactly today's list, with
    no server rows and no server-list call.
  - The desktop now advertises the relay capability, and routes a targeted `status.get` to the server.
  - The server workspace list drops its unread `stale`, `fetchedAt`, `totalCount` and `truncated`
    fields; the phone reads only the rows, and reads reachability from the server list.
- **Badge width.** The cap moved from the whole badge to the host name, so "· Update needed" stays
  readable.
- **Housekeeping.**
  - Adding the capability pushed `protocol-version.ts` over its 300-line cap. The two relay capabilities
    are one group in `mobile-desktop-relay-contract.ts`, and the account capabilities moved to
    `src/shared/account-runtime-capabilities.ts`, as the file's other groups already do. Same strings,
    same order.
  - The mobile page's script-count budget was re-measured for the new workspace modules: 79 scripts at
    16 routes.

## Why

The phone is meant to mirror its paired desktop, including servers. Setting the target once per
workspace route, rather than per call, keeps screens unaware of where they run. The desktop stays the
only reader of the routing table, so a phone and a desktop on different versions still agree. One feed
for the server list means the badge and the open workspace can't disagree, and the desktop is asked
once per tick, not once per screen.

Rejected alternatives:
- putting the target inside request params, which would avoid an app release but fork the relay contract;
- copying the routing table into the phone, which drifts when phone and desktop update separately;
- listing servers through the relay plus a cache, which means two listing paths;
- each screen polling the server list itself, which doubles the desktop's load and lets screens disagree.

## Linked Issue

N/A (maintainer)

## Visual Proof

![server-rows.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a7c3016d-2abc-451d-a150-1a5676081b5b)

This is a react-native-web render of the phone's list with stand-in icons, not a device capture. It shows
the update-needed notice, a server that needs an update, and a disconnected server with a long name.
The stack was also verified on an Android emulator against a real desktop and server.

## Testing

- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

- **End to end** (`tests/e2e/paired-mobile-desktop-mirror.spec.ts`) runs a real desktop, a real server
  and an encrypted phone client. The phone:
  - lists the server workspace through the desktop;
  - opens a server terminal and gets the computed output of `echo X_$((1000+7))`;
  - reads the server's files (`files.readDir`) and git status (`git.status`), while the same calls
    without a target fail on the desktop;
  - while the server is stopped, sees it reported as reconnecting and not relaying, still gets its last
    rows, and server calls return `remote_runtime_unavailable`;
  - after a restart, sees it relaying again and lists and works again.
  Removing the target from the phone's requests fails the test. Keystroke echo on one quiet machine was
  about 7 ms relayed against 6.5 ms direct.
- **Unit and wiring tests:**
  - the target on every transport (direct, cloud relay, bridge, replay, unsubscribe);
  - the envelope gate: a page under a shell without `rpcEnvelope` lists no server rows and makes no
    server-list call, and the same page with the grant lists them;
  - a census that renders all 14 workspace route files (native and web) and checks each passes the
    server down;
  - no desktop fallback;
  - the unreachable screen;
  - the connection state (connected, connecting, disconnected) and the shared feed (one read for two
    readers, polling past a slow read, discarding a reply from before a disconnect);
  - server feature gates;
  - pinning on the server;
  - hidden hosts;
  - old desktop and old shell showing today's view.
- **Relay integration:** a targeted `status.get` returns the server's runtime and capabilities.
- **Recorded RPC goldens:** 8 re-recorded with the recorder. The wire frames are byte-identical; only
  recorded screen state gains an empty server list and `visibleHostIds: null`.

## Notes

- **App release needed.** Phones need the app build that grants `rpcEnvelope` (#27815) to open server
  workspaces. The page side ships over the air and turns on once the shell grants it.
- **Wire compatibility:**
  - An old phone sends no target and sees today's list.
  - An old desktop doesn't advertise the relay, so the phone never targets it or calls its server list.
  - An old server is "Update needed".
- **SSH and folder workspaces:** unchanged, apart from following the desktop's hidden hosts.
- **Follow-ups in this stack:** server notification taps (#26518), New Workspace on a server and no
  Sleep on server rows (#26533), and browser pages the desktop draws for a server (#27749).
- The cloud-relay path is unit-tested but has no end-to-end test.

selected_prs.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 36 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1524 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​177 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1347 |
| Prod | 44 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​861 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​372 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​489 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Orca has two launcher entries for OpenCode: "OpenCode" (the `opencode` command) and "OpenCode 2" (the `opencode2` command). With Chat UI on, "OpenCode" opened Orca's chat view but "OpenCode 2" still opened a terminal, and on OpenCode 2.x the model picker stayed empty until the first message. Now OpenCode 2 opens as a chat, its models are listed before the first message, its skills show in the `/` menu, and a 2.x conversation from the terminal can be resumed in it.

## What Changed

**Before.**
- New tab > OpenCode 2 opened a terminal running `opencode2 --standalone`, even with Chat UI on.
- With `opencode` on 2.x, the picker had no models until the first message: Orca ran `opencode models --verbose`, which every 2.x release rejects.
- Resume in chat sent every 2.x conversation to the OpenCode chat. Where `opencode` is still 1.x, that chat showed the old messages, said it could not reopen the session, and started a new one.

**After.**
- OpenCode 2 opens as a chat when `opencode2` is a stable 2.x from 2.0.14. Anything else (older 2.x, a pre-release, 1.x, no `opencode2`) keeps the terminal.
- Both OpenCode chats list their models before the first message, per project: a project whose `opencode.json` adds or removes models shows its own list.
- A 2.x conversation resumes in the OpenCode 2 chat, or in the OpenCode chat when the host cannot run OpenCode 2.
- The `/` menu lists the skills OpenCode reads, and never lets a skill hide a command that OpenCode or Orca runs instead.

**Mechanism.**
- **Chat registration.** One OpenCode definition now serves both names. The `opencode2` row runs `opencode2 acp`, accepts 2.x only, and shares OpenCode's account, history rows and conversation import.
- **Models before the first message.** On 2.x the probe opens a session with `session/new` in the asking chat's folder, reads its models with the code a running chat uses, and deletes it with `session/delete`; an agent that cannot delete a session is not asked, a failed delete is logged, and a read with no folder stops before spawning anything. 1.x keeps `opencode models --verbose`, now run in the chat's folder. The startup and settings refreshes skip OpenCode, since they have no folder.
- **One model list per project.** For agents that list in a chat's folder (both OpenCode chats), the folder is part of the catalog key, a running chat saves its lists under its own folder in the order it reported them, and answers carry `modelsDifferByWorkspace` so the app's first-frame cache never shows one folder's list in another. Other agents keep one list per account.
- **One chat per conversation.** `opencode` and `opencode2` open the same conversations. Both single-writer checks (when a resume is asked for, and when the record is saved) now treat them as one conversation store, read from the shared table of which chats take over a Session History row. The stored handle format is unchanged.
- **Resume in chat.** That table now lists chats in order (`opencode2` rows: OpenCode 2, then OpenCode). The resume asks the host to admit the first and falls back to the next only when the host refuses it; a host that cannot answer yet keeps the first, whose own launch reports it.
- **Copying a chat for the CLI.** Resume in New CLI copies the conversation into this host's OpenCode store, so the CLI must not point at a server. The check now lives on the OpenCode launch spec, so it covers OpenCode 2 chats too, and the app checks every CLI whose chat could own the conversation before it asks for a copy.
- **Skills.** OpenCode chats list skills from the six folders OpenCode reads: its config folder, `~/.claude/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, and the project's `.opencode/skills`, `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills`. Claude's plugins are not offered. The scanned list stays after the first message, because 2.x reports no skills. A picked skill is sent as typed.
- **`/` menu precedence.** A command the chat's own send handles (`/compact`, `/clear`, `/model`, `/effort`) is never replaced by a same-named skill; this also fixes Claude's commands before its first report. An OpenCode command counts as the skill only when 1.x reported it under that skill's own description; any other clash shows the command with "Also a skill name".
- **Smaller tables.** OpenCode 2 is added to the sign-in hint, the project config files that decide a default model, the orchestration skill check, the chat permission modes and the phone app's icon. Notification titles now use the shared agent names, which also fixes about 17 agents that showed their raw id (for example `copilot`).

## Why

- **Why a separate OpenCode 2 chat, not the OpenCode one?** The OpenCode chat runs `opencode`. Where `opencode` is 1.x, that is the wrong program for a 2.x conversation.
- **Why a throwaway session for the model list?** 2.x's own listing commands are not reliable: every release rejects `--verbose`, and `opencode models` and `opencode api model.list` answer empty from a fresh start on 2.0.14 to 2.0.26 and missed a late provider on 2.0.28 (anomalyco/opencode#53682, #53724, #36117). A new session offers exactly what a chat offers, because it is how a chat starts. bb (get-bb/bb) does the same and also opens it in the chat's folder, since OpenCode 2 records a project for every folder a session opens in.
- **Why one list per folder?** A project's `opencode.json` can add or remove providers. bb keys OpenCode's list by folder for the same reason.
- **Why list skills from folders instead of asking OpenCode?** 2.x reports no skills over the chat protocol, and its skill list call answers empty on the first call after a start (anomalyco/opencode#51680, open). The folder rules are OpenCode's own; I checked them against 1.19 and 2.0.29.
- **Why send a picked skill as typed?** bb rewrites it into an instruction, but only for mentions its composer marks as skills, and it keeps its own copy of what it sent. Orca has neither, and rewriting broke crash recovery (which matches OpenCode's stored copy by text) and turned `/tmp is filling up` into a skill request.
- **Why no fallback to `opencode` when `opencode2` is missing at launch?** Same rule as any agent whose command is gone: new launches open the terminal, and an existing chat says it could not restart. The OpenCode 2 Command setting can point at `opencode`.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #19581

## Visual Proof

Before (main): New tab > OpenCode 2 opens a terminal.

![before-opencode2-terminal.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0fb1898b-a09b-460d-a9b7-664f41625b2f)

After: it opens a chat tab; a tool call, its output and the model picker are shown.

![after-opencode2-chat.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/22eb77c2-80f4-4db3-899e-b16c05908103)

A real OpenCode 2.0.29 chat with "Ask for approval" on, in a hidden dev build.

Permission card for a shell command:

![02-permission-card.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/12cc00a8-00ea-4ce8-a3cb-5cc895896022)

After "Allow once": the command ran and OpenCode replied with its output.

![03-tool-allowed-done.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e35dd436-2d89-4c91-ab91-d0b67aaca433)

After "Reject": OpenCode 2 ends the turn itself (`stopReason: "cancelled"`), shown as Interrupted. 1.x instead fails the tool and finishes the turn.

![05-rejected-done.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/45d67a32-fc45-44eb-b2dc-dffd9269b67d)

Stop during an approved `sleep 40`: the turn is Interrupted and the command's process is gone.

![07-stopped.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2f2ff414-2582-4624-bfd5-4d0bfd6dbe97)

After an app restart: the chat reopens with its history shown once.

![08-reopened.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/13278bc8-2c69-4d11-9e0f-1a1a1ed3498b)

A follow-up in the reopened chat: OpenCode loaded the same conversation and recalls the first command's output.

![09-reopened-follow-up.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f7ff8903-0c9d-4f12-aee9-a1cc44766683)

## Testing

Real app, hidden dev builds over the debugging port, macOS arm64, fresh profiles, OpenCode folders isolated from my own. OpenCode 1.18.35, 1.19.0, 1.19.1, 2.0.13, 2.0.14, 2.0.28 and 2.0.29.

- OpenCode 2 from the launcher with 2.0.28 and 2.0.14: chat tab. With 2.0.13: terminal.
- In an OpenCode 2 chat: reply, tool call row, Stop ("Interrupted", child process gone), permission card (Allow once and Reject), question tool (plain-text fallback), and the picked model is the one OpenCode's store says ran.
- Two OpenCode 2 chats at once: no messages crossed. Close and reopen from Session History, and app restart: same session, history shown once.
- Folder workspace (not git): the chat runs in the folder. Paired host: a client built from main against this host opens the chat; this client against a host built from main gets the terminal, as today.
- Models: 2.0.14 and 2.0.29 list 71 and 11 models before any message, with no session left in OpenCode's store and only the chat's folder in its project list. 1.19.0 lists through `models --verbose` with no session. After a restart, no OpenCode 2 refresh ran until a chat asked.
- One list per project: with `opencode` 1.19.1 and `opencode2` 2.0.29 sharing one database, project A listed 10 models and project B 11, including the model its `opencode.json` adds; Orca's trace shows one listing per folder.
- `/` menu: skills in each of the six folders are listed before and after the first message on 2.0.29, and once each on 1.19.0. With project skills named `compact` and `review`, the menu shows OpenCode's own commands with "Also a skill name". A picked skill, `/tmp is filling up` and `/review the branch` reach OpenCode as typed.
- Resume in chat with `opencode` 1.19.1 and `opencode2` 2.0.29: a 2.x terminal conversation opened in an OpenCode 2 chat with its history, showed no reopen warning, and the follow-up landed in the same conversation in OpenCode's store, with the agent recalling its earlier reply.
- Recorded OpenCode 2.0.29 traffic from a real chat in Orca, replayed through the chat code: an approved shell command, a rejected permission (2.x ends the turn as cancelled, unlike 1.x), Stop during a running command, and a reopen after restart whose `session/load` replays the history once before a follow-up.
- New tests, each failing without its change: the model-list session and its cleanup, one list per folder (sequential reads, simultaneous reads and a running chat's update), the 1.x listing folder, the first-frame cache, both single-writer checks in both directions and for two racing resumes, resume order and fallback (only on a refusal), a running chat's reports saved in order, copy refusal for both OpenCode CLIs, a 2.x terminal tab started as `opencode` handed to the OpenCode 2 chat, the `/` menu collisions for OpenCode and Claude, skill folders, notification names, launch limits and row ownership.
- `pnpm lint`, `pnpm tc`, the three audits, `check:code-quality:changed`, `check:react-doctor:changed`, `check:zustand-selector-fanout` and the mobile typecheck pass on the head. 300 dependent test files pass (3322 tests).

## Notes

- **Replaces #28423**, which this PR now includes.
- **Not tested:** Windows (there `opencode2` is a `.cmd` file), Linux, and the mobile app, so the phone icon is unseen. Mobile reads chat tabs for any agent the host lists, and the mobile typecheck and its chat tests pass.
- **Mixed versions:** one new optional field on the model list answer (`modelsDifferByWorkspace`); an older client ignores it, and an older host never sends it, so the first-frame cache behaves as today. No new stream message.
- **SSH and WSL workspaces:** unchanged; they keep the terminal for every agent.
- **Best effort cleanup:** a model-list session whose listing is stopped while OpenCode creates it can be left behind as one empty conversation, since there is no id to delete it by.
- **Overlap:** #25008 would list only "OpenCode 2" where both names are 2.x; this should land first, or those users lose the chat view.
- **Left for follow-ups:**
  - Question and form cards (OpenCode's question tool is off for now; 2.x then asks in plain text).
  - Using a picked skill by instruction, as bb does. That needs the composer to mark picked skills on the message and the chat's record to keep what was sent.
  - Skills in folders moved by `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`, and OpenCode's built-in skills, are not listed. Typing one still works.

selected_prs.body:

| Prod | 4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​32 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​25 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Antigravity chats need Google's separate Antigravity chat server. An earlier version of this stack downloaded it silently the first time a chat started: about 18 seconds of "Working for Ns" with no progress and no Cancel, and every extra chat opened started another download. Now nothing downloads until the person clicks Install, which shows the size, progress and Cancel in Settings and in the new chat.

This PR covers permissions. Some chat agents, Antigravity's server among them, enforce permissions themselves: Orca tells the agent which of its own modes to run in, and the agent decides when to ask. Main has a per-chat permission picker (Ask for approval, Accept edits, Approve for me, Full access), but Orca had no way to hand that choice to such an agent. This PR lets an agent map each picker choice to one of its own modes. No agent uses it yet; Antigravity (#28595) is the first.

## What Changed

**This revision** (moving to the common pattern): each agent's spec had to name its mode option's id (`configId`), so a server that renamed the option would have been sent the wrong one. The mode option is now found the way the common pattern finds it: the session's select option in the standard `mode` category, whatever the agent calls it (falling back to the id `mode`). Antigravity's option is `mode` in that category, so its behavior is unchanged.

- **Before:** nothing in Orca could hand an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) chat agent a per-chat permission mode. Under Full access, Orca approved the agent's permission requests on the person's behalf.
- **After:** an ACP launch spec can declare `permissionModeConfig`: the agent's own value for each Orca mode it supports, set on the session's `mode`-category option. An Ask value is required. Every start, new or reopened, sets the value for the chat's mode after restoring the chat's saved options. The start fails with "Permission mode could not be confirmed" if the agent doesn't report that value back. A chat with no mode, or with a mode the spec doesn't map, runs the Ask value, so the agent never gets more access than the person chose.
- **Changing the mode mid-chat:** no new code. The host already restarts a chat's agent before the next message when its mode changed (the same path Claude and Codex chats use), and that restart sets the new value.
- **Permission requests:** for an agent that enforces the mode itself, every permission request and question is shown to the person in every mode. Orca doesn't auto-approve them under Full access. The agent's own full-access mode decides what it still asks.
- **Merged alone:** no agent sets the field, so nothing changes.

## Why

The per-chat picker already owns the choice, where it is saved, and how a change reaches the host. Mapping that choice onto the agent's own modes reuses all of it: no second permission setting and no new message between client and host. Letting the agent enforce its own mode, rather than having Orca approve each request, keeps the agent's own rules about what counts as an edit and what counts as a command.

## Linked Issue

N/A (maintainer; part of the Antigravity Chat UI stack).

## Visual Proof

N/A: no agent sets the new field yet, so nothing visible changes. The picker for Antigravity arrives with #28595.

## Testing

- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

- One test through the real adapter, with an agent whose mode option has a non-standard id: a start in Accept edits sets the mapped value on that option, a start naming no mode requests the Ask value, and an agent that doesn't confirm the value fails the start. It fails if the chat's mode is ignored.
- `pnpm tc:node`, the ACP and shared test folders (13,835 tests) and the code-quality gate passed.

## Review

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Notes

- Mixed versions: the host owns both the mapping and the launch. An older client without an agent's picker row shows no picker, and the host still launches with the chat's saved mode, never the global setting.
- SSH and remote hosts: the mode is applied by the host that runs the chat.
- PR author: @BrennanKB5

### Differences from the common pattern

- Intended: if the agent does not confirm the requested mode, the chat start fails rather than running in whatever mode the agent kept. Antigravity's server restores a saved looser mode when a chat is reopened, so adopting whatever it reports could run a chat in Full access after the person chose Ask.
- Intended: a mode change takes effect by restarting the chat's agent before the next message, the path every other chat agent already uses, instead of a live mode switch. One permission-mode path for all agents; mode changes are rare.
- Intended: for an agent that enforces the mode itself, Orca shows every permission request it still sends instead of auto-approving it under Full access. In its own full-access mode Antigravity still asks only for reviews an administrator requires and for questions; approving those for the person would defeat that policy.

selected_prs.title: feat(acp): a sign-in prompt on an ACP agent's error output ends the start or turn signed out
selected_prs.body: | | Files | Added | Deleted | Net | | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​52 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​52 | | Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​95 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​42 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​53 | ## ELI5 Antigravity chats need Google's separate Antigravity chat server. An earlier version of this stack downloaded it silently the first time a chat started: about 18 seconds of "Working for Ns" with no progress and no Cancel, and every extra chat opened started another download. Now nothing downloads until the person clicks Install, which shows the size, progress and Cancel in Settings and in the new chat. This PR handles what that server does once installed but signed out. It doesn't answer "please sign in". It prints a sign-in link on its error output and then waits up to five minutes for someone to open it. Nobody sees that link in a chat, so the chat just hangs. With this PR an agent can declare "this line means I'm waiting for a browser sign-in". When Orca sees that line, the chat stops waiting right away and shows Orca's normal "not signed in" state. ## What Changed **This revision:** no code change. The differences list below was corrected: the per-agent matcher on the launch description is how the common pattern does it too, so it is no longer listed as a difference, and the long-line case is now listed. - **Before:** an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent that waits for a browser sign-in hangs the chat start until the agent's own timeout (five minutes for Antigravity's server). If it happened during a running turn, the turn ended as "unknown" and the chat as "agent exited". - **After:** an ACP launch spec can declare `signInPrompt(line)`. Orca reads that agent's error output line by line. On a match it closes the connection with its existing typed sign-in error, `AcpAuthRequiredError`. A chat start fails as not signed in, and a running turn fails the same way it does when the agent itself answers "sign in required". The matched line holds the sign-in link, so it never goes into the retained error tail, error messages or diagnostics. - **Merged alone:** no agent sets the field yet, so nothing visible changes. #28595 (Antigravity in Chat UI) is the first to set it. Mechanism: - `spawnManagedProviderProcess` takes an optional `onStderrLine(line): boolean` on the existing error-output drain. With it, output is split into complete lines and a line the callback claims is withheld from the tail. The pending partial line is capped at the tail size (8 KiB), so a long link split across chunks is still classified by its start. Without the callback, behaviour is unchanged. - The ACP connection passes the spec's matcher in and, on a match, closes through the existing process owner. - Mid-turn: the connection's close cause now reaches the turn tracker (`AcpStructuredTurns.end(reason, cause)`). When the cause is the sign-in error, the running turn takes the same failure path as a sign-in refusal from the agent (now one shared method) instead of settling "unknown". The helper for a send refused before it was written moved beside it as `rejectedAcpDispatch`, with no behaviour change. ## Why The common pattern for agents that sign in through a browser is to detect the waiting state and show a clear signed-out state, not to hang, and it does so the same way: a per-agent error-output handler handed to the generic agent runtime. Detecting the line through data on the launch spec keeps agent names out of shared code. Ending the turn through the existing sign-in failure path reuses what the chat already shows for "not signed in" rather than adding a new state. ## Linked Issue N/A (maintainer; part of the Antigravity Chat UI stack). ## Visual Proof This PR changes nothing visible on its own; the agent that sets the field arrives in a later PR. The result it produces was captured in a real run of the whole stack (M4Air, build `d871611d303`, a throwaway profile, nobody signed in, driven over the Chrome DevTools Protocol only): a message sent to a new Antigravity chat ended as "Your message was not sent. Sign in to Antigravity." instead of the chat waiting, and the sign-in link did not appear in the error text. This screenshot was taken before this PR's last review fix (long lines no longer keep their start in the saved error output). That fix is covered by a unit test, not by a screenshot. ## Testing - [x] I manually tested these changes locally - [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below - Connection test over the existing fixture process: a pending prompt, a noise line, then the sign-in line split across two chunks, with a link longer than the 8 KiB partial-line cap. The prompt rejects with the sign-in error, the process exits, the link appears in none of the error, diagnostics or retained tail, and the noise line is kept. - Session test: a running turn whose connection closes with the sign-in error settles as not signed in. It fails without the turn-tracker change. - `pnpm tc:node` and all ACP and provider-process tests (712) passed. The change is platform-independent. ## Review ## Agent skill upstream boundary - [x] Not applicable, or this change copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation. ## Notes - Accepted edge: if the agent exits before its buffered sign-in output is read, the start reports the agent exit. The matched sign-in line is still withheld from retained output. - Security: the sign-in link is kept out of every retained or reported string. - After a mid-turn sign-in close the session also ends, because the process is closed, so the host also reports an ended session. At chat start, QA on #28595 saw one signed-out notice and no second "agent exited" error. The mid-turn case has not been checked live. - No SSH, mobile or wire impact: detection runs on the host that runs the agent. - PR author: @BrennanKB5 ### Differences from the common pattern - Intended: a line counts as a sign-in prompt by its prefix alone; the link itself is never parsed or used, because chats sign in through a separate flow (#28650). The common pattern ignores a prompt line whose link fails its own check, and the server then waits up to five minutes for a browser, so that chat start hangs; here it ends signed out at once. - Intended: a very long partial line is still recognised by its start, where the common pattern drops lines over 16 KiB and the same five-minute wait follows. - Intended: only the error output is watched. The pinned server prints its sign-in prompt only there on purpose, because its standard output carries the protocol, and Orca runs only a copy that matches every pinned file. The common pattern also scans standard output because it can run other builds from a custom path. - Intended: the rest of the error output is still kept for failure details; only the line holding the link is dropped. Orca's shared error-output tail feeds failure details for every agent. - Intended: the result is the chat's existing "not signed in" failure on that send or start, not a signed-out flag for the whole agent, because each host keeps its own sign-in. ## ELI5

Antigravity chats need Google's separate Antigravity chat server. An earlier version of this stack downloaded it silently the first time a chat started: about 18 seconds of "Working for Ns" with no progress and no Cancel, and every extra chat opened started another download. Now nothing downloads until the person clicks Install, which shows the size, progress and Cancel in Settings and in the new chat, and Settings can also remove the download again.

All Antigravity chats on one machine share one Google sign-in and one installed server. If a chat keeps running while you sign in to another account, the server can quietly save the old sign-in back over the new one. If it keeps running while the server is removed, it runs files that are being deleted. This PR adds a short pause around those changes: while one runs, new Antigravity chats are refused with a clear message, chats still starting are cancelled, and every server process is proven stopped before the change begins.

## What Changed

**This revision:** the gate missed one way the server starts. When a chat is opened in the agent's own terminal program, Orca first has the server save a copy of the conversation, and that copy started the server with the shared sign-in folder outside the gate, so a sign-in change could run while that server still held the old sign-in. Conversation copies now enter the gate like a chat start, and the gate holds each copy's server until it exits. This was in #29139 before; it moved here so this PR covers every process it claims to on its own.

- **Before:** nothing coordinated chat starts with a change to an agent's shared sign-in or installed server.
- **After:** an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent's launch spec can carry a launch gate (`AcpLaunchGate`). It lives in memory only and always releases when the operation ends.
  - Every chat start, and every conversation copy, enters the gate first. While an operation runs, a new start is refused as "account changing" (the existing `accountSwitchInProgress` reason).
  - When an operation begins, starts under way are aborted, and the gate waits for them to leave. The operation then stops the running chats it names.
  - The gate also holds every server process it let start, a conversation copy's included, until that process exits. A start leaves the gate once its process is up, but the host lists the chat as running only after it finishes attaching, so a stop that only looked at running chats would miss a chat in that window. Before the operation's work runs, the gate closes each process it still holds, and each must prove it exited.
  - If a chat or process can't be proven stopped, the operation fails without running: "Antigravity could not be stopped on this host. Try again."
- The existing refusal message now names whichever agent it is about and covers every setup change the gate fences. It used to say "A Claude account switch is in progress. Try again after it finishes." and now says "{{agent}}'s setup is changing on this host. Try again after it finishes." in all six languages. Claude's existing account switch now reads "Claude's setup is changing on this host. Try again after it finishes."
- Antigravity sets the gate; no other agent does. The operations that use it are the chat sign-in (#28650) and removing the downloaded server (#29139). Merged alone, nothing runs an operation, so the only visible change is the message wording.

## Why

The Antigravity server writes its sign-in back to its folder every time it refreshes it, so a chat left running would undo a sign-in. A chat left running during Remove would run deleted files. Stopping every process before the change, and refusing new starts while it runs, closes both windows with one fence instead of a lock per operation. Like the common pattern, every path that starts this agent goes through it. Holding each started process until it exits, rather than trusting the list of loaded chats, covers the gap between a start and its attach. Reusing the existing account-change refusal keeps one message for one situation, and older paired Orca versions already understand that reason.

N/A (maintainer; part of the Antigravity Chat UI stack).

## Visual Proof

N/A: nothing triggers the gate until #28650 (sign-in) or #29139 (Remove). The message change is copy only.

- Through the existing adapter rig: a start under way when an operation begins is aborted before the operation's work runs, a new start during the operation is refused with the account-changing reason, and an operation whose chat stop fails never runs its work. It fails without the adapter hook.
- An operation started while a chat has started but is not yet loaded stops that chat's process before the work runs.
- `pnpm tc:node`, `pnpm tc:web` and the ACP and runtime tests passed.
