### Differences from the common pattern

- Intended: a sign-in change (and later a runtime removal) proceeds only once every process of the agent is proven to have exited; if any cannot be, the change fails and the person can try again. The common pattern waits for its stop without proof of exit. A close that cannot prove exit is not evidence the process is gone, and the change must not replace or delete files under a process that may still use them.
- Intended: the gate is entered by chat starts and conversation copies, the sign-in process runs inside the gated operation itself, and Orca starts no model-listing or background process for this agent. The common pattern hands the same lock to every one of its consumers; the coverage is the same, through Orca's start paths.
- Intended: there is one gate per agent per host, because Orca keeps one sign-in folder per agent per host and has no per-provider instances.

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

When a chat ran into Claude's 5-hour or weekly usage limit (or Codex's), Orca treated it like a crash: a red error row quoting the provider's raw text, sometimes twice, and nothing saying which limit it was, when it resets, or how to carry on. Now the chat says it plainly, for example "Claude hit its session limit. It resets at 3:00 PM.", in a calm warning style, with a **Continue** button that picks the turn back up.

## What Changed

**Before**
- Claude: the CLI's "You've hit your limit · resets 3pm" showed as an ordinary assistant message, then again as a red error row. Claude's typed limit report (which limit, when it resets) was thrown away.
- Codex: its usage reports were dropped, and the turn-ending error printed Codex's own message as a red row.
- Grok: "Grok usage limit reached." in red, with no reset time.
- In every case the only way on was to type a new message.

**After**
- One warning row per limited turn. It names the limit (session, weekly, weekly model, extra usage) and shows the reset time in the reader's own clock. The provider's own words are kept with the row's details.
- The warning stays visible when the finished turn is collapsed, the same way a failed turn's error row does today; the agent's work above it stays folded.
- **Continue** sits on that row while it is the chat's latest turn and nothing has been sent since. It sends "Continue where you left off." as your message, so the agent carries on in the same conversation, with your current model and effort and no attachments. Whatever you were typing (and any attached images) stays in the composer untouched; an old composer error clears; the view scrolls to the new message; keyboard focus lands in the composer. If the limit hasn't reset yet, the agent simply hits it again and says so.
- If another window or device has already continued the chat or sent something newer, that Continue is refused instead of sending a second continuation, and the composer says the chat has moved on.
- The phone shows the same sentence and reset time (it has no Continue, just as it has none for a reply cut off by an Orca restart today).
- Older desktop clients and older phones keep working: they show the host's sentence ("Claude hit its session limit. Send a message once it resets to continue.") in the warning style.

**Mechanism**
- Shared: a new `usageLimitReached` failure fact, optionally carrying `usageLimit: { window, resetsAt }`, worded by the shared failure-sentence table like every other failure Orca reports. An older client doesn't know the kind, drops the fact and shows the row's text, which is already a full sentence.
- Claude (`claude-usage-limits.ts`, `claude-terminal-failure.ts`): reads the typed limit from the API-error frame (`api_error: usage_limit_reached` with its `rate_limit_info`). Failing that, a refusal can use the latest `rate_limit_event` that reports a limit as `rejected` with no paid usage to fall back on. Each rejection stands until a later reading allows that limit again or its reset passes, because the CLI does not repeat an unchanged rejection on every turn. The turn's own typed error always wins over that remembered rejection: a different typed refusal stays an ordinary failure. A bare `error: rate_limit` alone is **not** treated as a usage limit (the CLI uses it for temporary throttles and policy refusals too), and neither is a `blocking_limit` end, which the CLI only produces for "Prompt is too long". The warning is one row owned by the open turn, so the API-error frame and the failed result update the same row instead of adding a second one, and a limited turn that ends without a result frame (idle or the CLI exiting) is still saved as failed with Continue, unless you pressed Stop.
- Codex (`codex-usage-limits.ts`): keeps the latest `account/rateLimits/updated` report, merging partial updates and reusing the status bar's window classifier. The turn-ending `usageLimitExceeded` / `rateLimitExceeded` error then becomes the limit row. The reset is the latest one among the spent windows.
- ACP: the `rate_limit` stop reason (Grok) writes the same fact, without a reset time, because Grok doesn't send one.
- Continue: worked out from the chat history each time, never stored: the latest turn failed, one of its rows is a usage limit, and nothing has been sent since. The scan that finds the latest turn is now shared with the restart Continue. The click goes through the composer's ordinary send (`agentSession.send`), with the same completion as typing and sending a message (takeover of a worker chat, scroll to newest, error cleared), but it never reads or clears your draft.
- Continue is tied to its turn: when the host advertises `agent-session.send-usage-limit-continuation.v1`, the send carries an optional `usageLimitContinuationOfTurnItemId`. The host replays an already-recorded send first, then checks, before anything is queued, that this is still the latest limited turn and the chat is idle; otherwise it refuses with nothing sent. A host without the capability gets the exact plain send it gets today. The field is part of the operation's identity, not the message, so ordinary sends hash exactly as before.
- Details: the row's Details disclosure now shows the provider's saved explanation even when no raw provider frame was kept (Claude and ACP).

## Why

- **The common pattern** classifies a provider failure by kind, with the reset time attached to the failed turn, and offers a resume that is a plain "Continue where you left off." message. This PR adopts that mechanism rather than rewording the red row for each agent.
- **Why a plain message for Continue, not Orca's restart-continuation path:** that path's wording and notes all say Orca restarted. A plain message is visibly yours in the transcript and still works with older paired servers. Like the common pattern, the message names the turn it continues and the host checks it, so two windows (or a phone and a desktop) can't both continue the same turn; that check is behind a new capability so older servers keep the plain send.
- **Why keep the turn marked failed:** the turn did fail, the common pattern keeps it failed too, and the sidebar and agent-status readers stay unchanged.

**Intended differences from the common pattern**
- A bare `rate_limit` error is not counted as a usage limit, as explained above (the CLI's own SDK schema says those other refusals never carry the limit details).
- The host never writes a clock time or a countdown into the saved text. The host may be an SSH or paired server in another time zone, and a saved countdown goes stale.
- A Claude `blocking_limit` end is not counted as a usage limit. In the Claude CLI (2.1.270 through 2.1.302) its only source is the pre-send "Prompt is too long" check, so treating it as a usage limit would offer a Continue that cannot work.
- Claude's remembered account rejection is kept across turns instead of collected per turn, because the CLI suppresses repeats of an unchanged rejection.
- Monthly or unrecognized Codex windows get the generic wording with their reset time rather than a guessed window name, so older readers can still show the reset.

**Not in this PR**
- Automatic Continue at reset time. Defaults differ (off by default with a per-chat switch, or on by default), so this needs a product decision.
- A "usage limit" label in the sidebar or `worktree ps`. That belongs to the agent-status store and needs terminal agents to report it too.
- Holding queued messages while a chat is limited.
- Codex releases older than 0.148: a turn that never opened is still settled as a refused send, in Codex's words.

## Linked Issue

Tracked in the native-chat audit (usage limits read as failures). No GitHub issue.

## Visual Proof

Real Electron QA on the M4Air at f7ab34c (main at 613c5986 for comparison). The usage limit is a replay of the Claude CLI's real frame shapes through a stand-in CLI, because a real limit can't be triggered safely; the normal chats use the real signed-in Claude and Codex CLIs.

selected_prs.title: fix(native-chat): save a Codex message's receipt from either of Codex's reports of it, not only the first
selected_prs.body:
## ELI5

When Codex takes a message you sent, it repeats the message's id back to Orca, and Orca writes that down as proof the message arrived. Today Orca only tries to write it down once. If that one write fails, the proof is lost, even though Codex repeats the id a second time a moment later. This change lets Orca use either of Codex's repeats, so one failed write no longer loses the proof.

## What Changed

**The problem.** Codex reports every message it records twice, back to back: once when it starts recording it and once when it finishes. Each report carries the message's id. Orca saves the first report as the message's receipt, the record that says "Codex got this". But Orca decided whether a receipt was still owed from an in-memory list of sends it was waiting on, and the first report removes the send from that list. So if the first save failed (a rare failed database write), the second report found nothing waiting and was ignored. The failure was only logged.

What a user saw in that case: the message never got its confirmation, and after a Stop, sending a message directly did not lift the pause on queued messages; they stayed held.

**The user-facing change.**
- When Codex reports a message's id, Orca records the message as received even if the first save failed: Codex's second report retries it.
- After a Stop, sending a message directly now lifts the paused queue in that case too, the same as it already does when the first save succeeds.
- Nothing else changes: no new label, row or wording. Withdrawn, refused and failed messages stay that way even if a report of them arrives later.

**The mechanism.** Orca still releases the send from its in-memory list on each exact report of its id; that is what tells the chat Codex is no longer holding it. Both reports are now passed on, and the chat's saved history decides whether a receipt is still owed, at the moment the write reaches its turn in the chat's write queue: the receipt is written only if the message is still waiting for a delivery answer, so two reports save once. This decision lives in the shared late-receipt path used by every agent, so for Claude, Pi and ACP agents too, a repeated receipt for a message that is already settled no longer writes an extra (ignored) saved row or sends clients an identical update.

Changed files: `codex-structured-session-journal.ts` (pass on both reports), `journal-submission-writer.ts` and `journal-store.ts` (the one "accept if still owed" write), and `structured-agent-session-late-dispatch.ts` (route late receipts to it).

## Why

Earlier revisions of this PR built much more: a saved "every receipt for this turn is complete" marker, a saved "which turn answered this message" row, a record of who ended each turn, a saved prompt-hook reason, and an in-memory retention list whose entries were re-saved with the turn's end and when Codex exited. All of that existed so Orca could one day conclude "not sent" from a missing receipt. The decision since then is that Orca never says "not sent" because a receipt is missing; a message counts as sent only on Codex's exact report of its id. With that ruling none of those pieces has a reader, so this PR removes all of them before they ship. No new saved field or wire change remains.

Two narrower designs were considered. Keeping a separate retry list for failed receipt saves was rejected: the common pattern keeps the receipt in one place and clears remaining doubt later from the agent's own history, which is needed anyway for a crash before any save. Checking "still owed" in the Codex adapter when the report arrives (an earlier revision of this rework) was also rejected: the check ran before the write reached the queue, so two reports arriving while the queue was busy could both write, and it needed extra plumbing and a test-only fallback. Deciding inside the queued write is smaller and has one source of truth.

**Known gaps (unchanged from main).** A receipt whose save fails on both reports, a crash before any save, and a report Orca could not read at all leave the message without a confirmation, exactly as today. They are cleared by the planned positive replay of Codex's history.

**Differences from the common pattern:**
- The receipt is saved to the chat's history. **Intended**: several clients, phones and an Orca restart read the saved history; in-memory state reaches none of them.
- A receipt whose saves all fail stays unconfirmed until a positive replay of Codex's history. **Temporary**: removed by the planned positive-replay change.
- When Codex's history is replayed (at reopen on older servers, and at rewind), replayed messages are still confirmed by their text rather than by the id they carry, and two identical-text messages can confirm the wrong one. This is existing behavior for all agents, not changed here. **Temporary**: removed by the planned positive confirmation by exact id.
- The in-memory "not sent" verdicts for interrupted or failed turns stay. **Temporary**: removed together with the planned "couldn't confirm whether this was sent" recovery action.

## Linked Issue

Part of the native-chat send lifecycle work, after #29907 and #29922. Not a GitHub issue.

## Visual Proof

Nothing new is drawn; these show the changed flows look the same on main and on this branch. Real Electron QA with the real Codex CLI in the chat view, on macOS (driven by an automated QA agent) and on Windows (send, steer, Stop then a direct send, quit and reopen). The main side is the commit this branch started from; the branch side is this PR's head. On both, every message got exactly one saved receipt and no duplicates. A failed first save can't be forced in the real app; the held-sends test covers it.

| Flow | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send, completes | ![main-f1.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/56c59ee6-649c-4808-ba3e-ab1a30c793a6) | ![pr-f1.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/37f865e5-3731-442a-99bd-8858846fea0b) |
| /compact, then send | ![main-f5.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6988b9fd-cbb9-4a28-829d-03872e7eba8f) | ![pr-f5.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a955fcf4-140b-41d1-862a-c3ba4a63a450) |
| Stop mid-turn, then send directly | ![main-f3.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/23a0f968-8614-4f72-ac5c-01da4aa8d59a) | ![pr-f3.jpg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/110fbd13-bc7b-4bd6-bb4d-1e36e263081c) |

The queued-message flows couldn't be exercised: the message queue is switched off in this build, so a send during a reply steers it instead.

## Testing

- `structured-agent-session-codex-held-sends.test.ts`, through the shipped host, journal and Codex adapter with only the Codex process faked: one send, Codex reports it twice (started, then completed), and the first receipt save is made to fail. The send is still waiting after the first report and accepted after the second, in the host's saved record and in what clients receive. Fails on main.
- `structured-agent-session-late-settlement.test.ts`: two identical receipts at once plus a different one for an accepted send add no saved row (main wrote three); a receipt that arrives after a send was withdrawn leaves it withdrawn.
- Codex adapter tests that pinned "a report for an unsent, refused or settled send is not passed on" were updated: that rule now lives in the shared write, covered by the tests above.

- Mobile: reads the same saved receipt.

| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​85 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​120 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​35 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Orca estimates what your Claude usage would cost at API prices. When Anthropic released Sonnet 5.5, Orca didn't know its price and quietly used Sonnet 5's instead, which charges twice as much for cached tokens. Haiku 5.5 was worse: Orca knew no price at all and counted it as free, with no hint that the total was incomplete. This PR makes Orca look up each model's exact price, and say so when it can't.

## What Changed

**Before**
- Sonnet 5.5 usage was priced as Sonnet 5, with cache reads at $0.20 instead of $0.10 per million tokens. Claude Code sessions are mostly cache reads, so the estimate ran high (about 29% on a typical mix).
- Haiku 5.5 usage added $0, and the Claude cost card showed a normal-looking total.
- Any future point release such as `opus-5-6` or `fable-5-2` would have been priced as the older model, again silently.

**After**
- Sonnet 5.5 has its own price row. Mythos 5 and 5.1 are priced at their Fable equivalents.
- A model with no exact price row is left out of the total, and the Claude cost card and Overview say so ("• excludes unpriced models"), as Codex already does (#22073).
- Several older names that came back with no price are now priced: `claude-3-7-sonnet-…`, `claude-3-haiku-…`, and Cursor-style `claude-4.5-sonnet`. Bedrock's dated Opus 4 id (`us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-20250514-v1:0`) was priced as Opus 4.8 and now gets Opus 4 rates. Dated Sonnet 4 ids now get Sonnet 4's row, so its over-200K pricing tier applies.

**How it works:** `normalizeModelForPricing` used to be a long ordered list of patterns, and a new version fell through to whichever older pattern matched first. It now reads the family, major and optional minor version out of the id; both `claude-sonnet-4-5` and the legacy `claude-3-5-sonnet` forms are handled. Date stamps, `[1m]`, `-thinking`, Bedrock and Vertex wrappers are ignored. It then accepts only an exact key in `MODEL_PRICING`. Adding a model is now a single table row. The Claude summary gains `hasUnpricedModels`, and both usage panes use one shared `unpricedCostLabel` helper for the note.

**Behaviour change:** the old rule that priced unknown Opus 4.x as Opus 4.8 and unknown Sonnet 4.x as Sonnet 4.6 is removed. Those versions never shipped, and the rule was the same silent-fallback pattern that caused this bug.

**Not in this PR: Haiku 5.5 stays unpriced, and flagged.** It charges a higher rate on the *whole request* once the prompt is over 100K tokens. Orca adds up Claude usage per day before pricing, so it can't tell which requests crossed that line. Pricing it properly needs per-request tracking, which Codex already has (#22360). That is a follow-up.

## Why

Adding one row for Sonnet 5.5 would have fixed this ticket, but the next release would break the same way. This is the fifth report of this kind, after GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol and Sonnet 5.5. Matching only exact versions turns a silently wrong number into a total that is visibly marked incomplete. A test checks that every row in the price table is found by its own name.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #30338 (STA-11064)

## Visual Proof

Not captured. The only visible change is the existing Codex note "• excludes unpriced models" now also appearing on the Claude cost card and in the Overview's existing partial-cost line, when the selected range includes a model with no price. The renderer change is a shared helper that already-tested Codex code now calls.

## Testing

- [x] Automated tests added/updated
- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally (not run in the app)

- `claude-model-pricing.test.ts`: every price-table row resolves to itself; about 20 real id formats (dated, Bedrock, Vertex, `[1m]`, `-thinking`, legacy and Cursor-style); unknown versions stay unpriced; Sonnet 5.5 rates.
- `claude-usage-report-aggregation.test.ts`, `store.test.ts`, `usage-overview-model.test.ts`: the unpriced flag in the Claude summary and in the Overview total.
- Locally: `pnpm tc`, oxlint, oxfmt and `check:code-quality:changed` pass. The claude-usage, codex-usage, stats, automations and store-slice suites (471 files) ran with one failure, a store test still expecting the removed Opus 4.x → 4.8 fallback; I rewrote it for the new rule and it passes on its own. The full set was not re-run afterwards.
- I compared old and new resolver results on about 105 model ids. No id that main priced correctly now gets a different price.

Platform-independent pricing logic in the main process. SSH: no change; this reads local Claude transcripts only. Compatibility: `hasUnpricedModels` is a new field on a local IPC summary; if it is missing it reads as false. Performance: at most two regex runs per daily row, fewer than before.

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

> Stacked on #30421. Review and merge that first; this PR's diff is only the second commit.

## ELI5

Claude Haiku 5.5 charges about five times more for a request whose prompt is over 100K tokens. Orca only kept a running total of tokens per day, so it couldn't tell which requests were big. That's why #30421 left Haiku 5.5 unpriced. Now Orca checks each request's size as it reads the logs and remembers how many tokens came from big ones. Haiku 5.5 gets a correct price.

## What Changed

**Before**
- Haiku 5.5 had no price; after #30421 the Claude cost card said "excludes unpriced models".
- The older Sonnet 4.5 / Sonnet 4 surcharge for requests over 200K was worked out from each day's totals. A day of many small requests that added up past 200K was overcharged. A single real 500K request was undercharged, because only the part above 200K got the higher rate. This is the same bug Codex had and fixed in #22360 (STA-8117).

**After**
- Haiku 5.5 is priced: $0.10 / $0.50, and $0.50 / $2.50 for requests over 100K. Cache rates are on the same scale.
- Sonnet 4.5 / 4 apply their surcharge only to requests that were actually over 200K, and to the whole request.
- Day-by-day totals and the Usage screen layout don't change; only the cost estimates do.

**How it works**
- **Per-request check.** When a request is read from the transcript, `longContextTurnTokens` checks its prompt size (input plus cache reads and writes) against that model's threshold from `MODEL_PRICING`. If it is over, the request's tokens are also added to a `longContext` field on the daily and per-location rows. The field only appears on rows that had such a request, so rows for other models stay the same size.
- **Growing requests.** Claude Code logs the same request several times as it streams. If a later copy pushes a request over the threshold, the resume correction moves the whole request into `longContext`.
- **Pricing.** `estimateCostUsd(model, tokens)` takes one token object and prices the `longContext` part at the higher rates and the rest at normal rates. This replaces the old per-bucket tiering and its "shared allowance across cache TTLs" workaround.
- **Rebuilding old data.** Each saved per-file result now records `projectionVersion`. The scanner reparses any file saved by an older version, so existing history gets the new field on the next scan.

## Why

- **Why per request:** it's how Anthropic bills, and the same approach Codex already uses (#22360). The alternative was pricing Haiku 5.5 at its normal rate and undercounting big requests silently, which is the kind of quiet error #30421 removes.
- **Why a per-file version instead of bumping the cache schema:** the Claude cache schema version (6 and 7) also controls cache signing and migration, with tests for forged and legacy files. Bumping it for a pricing change would have meant rewriting that security logic. The per-file version only decides whether a file is reparsed, and the next change of this kind just bumps the number. It is deliberately kept out of the file's integrity hash, because hashing it would make caches saved by older builds fail validation and show users an error.

## Linked Issue

Follow-up to #30338 (STA-11064), stacked on #30421.

## Visual Proof

N/A. No UI change; only the dollar amounts the existing cost cards show.

## Testing

- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally (not run in the app)

- `scanner-long-context.test.ts`, using real transcript files and the real scanner:
  - only requests over their own model's threshold are recorded: Haiku 5.5 at 101K yes, 99K no; Sonnet 4.5 at 151K no; Sonnet 4.6 at 501K no, since it has no surcharge;
  - a resumed request that grows from 91K to 121K moves into the long-context subset, and the result matches a fresh full scan;
  - a file saved by an older version is reparsed.
- I checked the last two tests catch breakage: each fails when its mechanism is disabled.
- `claude-model-pricing.test.ts`: Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 4.5 long-context rates; a day's total over 200K stays at the normal rate; models without a surcharge ignore the subset; a subset larger than its totals is capped.
- `claude-usage-report-aggregation.test.ts`: summary and per-model breakdown price Haiku 5.5's long-context subset.
- Locally: `pnpm tc`, oxlint, oxfmt and `check:code-quality:changed` pass. The claude-usage, usage, automations and stats suites pass (82 files, 691 tests).

- **Sonnet 4.5's 200K threshold:** Anthropic's current pricing page no longer lists the Sonnet 4.5 / 4 long-context tier. The threshold and rates are carried over unchanged, and the whole-request reading follows how Anthropic described that tier when it was listed.
- **Automation run costs:** priced from session location totals with the session's model, as before. The long-context share follows each request's own model.

## ELI5

Orca had two copies of the code that types "you have new mail" into an agent's terminal. Only the newer copy was ever called. This deletes the old copy and the bookkeeping that only it used.

## What Changed

**Before / after for users:** nothing changes. The deleted code could not run.

**Mechanism:** when an orchestration message arrives for an agent running in a terminal, Orca types a short pointer ("check your mail") into that terminal and presses Enter. That job is done by `OrchestrationMailboxPointerDelivery` (`mailbox-pointer-delivery.ts`, `mailbox-pointer-stage.ts`, `mailbox-pointer-submit.ts`). It records each step in the orchestration database so delivery survives a restart.

An older version of the same job, `deliverPendingMessages` in `orchestration/mail/terminal-message-delivery.ts`, was still part of the runtime class chain. Its only callers were itself (after a liveness probe) and `settlePendingMessageDelivery`, and that method's only caller was `deliverPendingMessages`. Nothing outside that pair, including tests, reached either of them.

Removed:
- the old delivery class, plus its link in the runtime class chain. `OrcaRuntimeWithResolveWaiter` now extends the next class, `OrcaRuntimeWithResolveExitWaiters`, directly;
- `settlePendingMessageDelivery` and the abstract `deliverPendingMessages` declaration;
- state that only the old path read or wrote: in-flight deliveries, parked redeliveries, probe dedupe, and the per-mailbox "already pointed" watermark and id set;
- `isCursorAgentOrchestrationTarget` and `RuntimeMessageWaiters.typeHasLiveWaiter`, whose only caller was the old path;
- a code comment that named the old function now points at mailbox pointer delivery.

## Why

Dead code that looks live misleads readers. We found this while planning a shared "submit text to an agent terminal" helper: the old file looked like the obvious place to extract from, but it never runs. Deleting it removes about 265 lines and a link in the runtime class chain, with no behaviour to preserve. The alternative, leaving it and documenting it as unused, keeps the trap in place.

selected_prs.body:

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 12 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​921 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​911 |
| Prod | 26 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1311 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​53 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1258 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

If your Orca app is connected to a remote Orca server, the Claude and Codex **Add Account** buttons were greyed out. The only way to add an account was to open a terminal on the server and run `orca account add`. Now the button works: the server runs the sign-in, and this device just opens the sign-in page. For Codex you type in the one-time code it shows. For Claude you paste back the code the page shows after you sign in.

## What Changed

- **Before:** with the default runtime (or the Settings host picker) set to a remote server, Add Account was disabled for both Claude and Codex. The note under it only said "add or re-authenticate accounts on that server", without saying how.
- **After:** Add Account starts a sign-in **on the server**. A panel under the button shows:
  - **Codex:** the OpenAI device page (Open / Copy link) and the one-time code (Copy code). Once you finish on that page, the account shows up in the server's list.
  - **Claude:** the Claude sign-in page (Open / Copy link) and a box for the code the page shows after you sign in. The code goes to the server, which finishes the login.
  - Cancel stops the login on the server.

How it works:
- The server runs the same CLI logins `orca account add` already uses: `claude auth login --claudeai` and `codex login --device-auth`. Their output and stdin are piped instead of attached to a terminal. The link (and for Codex, the code) is read from a captured transcript of each CLI's output. A link or code that comes from anywhere other than the provider's own sign-in host is ignored.
- The server reuses its existing account registration: Claude's per-account folder sign-in, and Codex's managed-home add. The credentials never leave the server. The client only sees the page address and the Codex code, and only sends the pasted Claude code.
- There are four new RPC methods: `accounts.hostSignInStart`, `accounts.hostSignInWait` (a long poll, at most 20 seconds per call), `accounts.hostSignInSubmitCode` and `accounts.hostSignInCancel`. A sign-in belongs to the paired device that started it: no other client can read it, answer it or cancel it. The server runs one at a time. If the client stops polling for 90 seconds (it closed, slept or lost its connection), the server ends the sign-in so the server's account queue isn't left waiting on it.
- The capability `accounts.host-sign-in.v1` controls who uses this. A client talking to an older server gets "update Orca on that server, or run `orca account add` there" instead of a request the server doesn't know. Older clients never call the new methods.
- Windows servers refuse for now. Their `claude`/`codex` logins run in a console window of their own, so their input and output can't be piped. Those users get the `orca account add` guidance.
- "Copy sign-in link instead" is hidden in remote scope, because that link calls back to localhost on the server.

## Why

The login has to run on the server: that is where the account folder and the credentials live, which is why the add methods only accepted the server's own callers. But nothing requires the person to be at the server. Both CLIs already support a sign-in finished on another device: Claude's pasted-code link and Codex's device code. So the server runs the process, and the client shows the link and passes the code back. tobolik proposed this design in the issue. It follows the pattern Orca already uses for Antigravity chat sign-in (start, cancel and complete, tied to the caller), but uses a long poll instead of a stream, which keeps the client simpler.

Alternatives considered:
- Keep the button disabled and name the CLI command (the approach in #20043). That explains the problem but doesn't fix it, and main already disables the button with similar guidance.
- Forward Claude's localhost callback through the client. That needs a tunnel and only works for Claude.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #20009

Thanks to @LucasOliveira-dev2026 for the report and the server-side diagnosis. Thanks to @shaggydo0 and @tobolik for the diagnostics and the device/paste-code design, and to @denis-sj for #20043, whose guidance approach this replaces.

## Visual Proof

Not attached. The flow needs a paired remote server, and this is noted in Testing.

## Testing

- New unit tests (they fail on main, where the methods don't exist and the remote-scope buttons are disabled):
  - `src/main/runtime/host-account-sign-in-flows.test.ts`: passing the link and code, owner isolation, cancel, failure messages, the silence watchdog, the Windows refusal.
  - `src/main/claude-accounts/claude-pasted-code-login.test.ts`: parsing a captured Claude 2.1.306 transcript, writing to stdin, the message for a refused code, cancel.
  - `src/main/codex-accounts/codex-device-auth-prompt.test.ts`: parsing a captured codex-cli 0.163.0 transcript.
  - `src/main/codex-accounts/service-device-code-login.test.ts`: the service adds an account through `--device-auth`.
  - `src/main/runtime/rpc/methods/accounts.test.ts`: a paired device's flow through the RPC methods, and a second device being refused.
  - `src/renderer/src/components/settings/AccountsPane.test.tsx`: both remote-scope Add Account buttons are enabled.
  - `src/renderer/src/runtime/runtime-host-account-sign-in-client.test.ts`: pairing pin, a Cancel at every stage, joining a running sign-in, a cancel that is asked again, and the retry policy (with fake timers).
  - `src/main/claude-accounts/claude-command-process.test.ts`: EPIPE on stdin.
- New opt-in real-CLI test `src/main/claude-accounts/host-sign-in-real-cli.test.ts` (`ORCA_REAL_CLAUDE_CLI_TEST=1` / `ORCA_REAL_CODEX_CLI_TEST=1`): it ran on the final head (4fe8dd7) locally on macOS against Claude Code 2.1.306 and codex-cli 0.163.0, and both cases **passed** (Claude: link published, bogus code refused with exit 1; Codex: device page and code parsed, cancel stopped the process).
- **Verified live (macOS, real CLIs, throwaway config folders):** the real `claude auth login --claudeai` printed its pasted-code link, which the new code picked up. A bogus code written to its stdin was refused with the new message (Claude prints the link on stdout, does not re-prompt, and exits 1). The real `codex login --device-auth` printed the device page and code, which were parsed, and Cancel killed the process. No processes or folders were left behind.
- **Only in tests:** the RPC round trip between a paired client and a real `orca serve`, the renderer panel, and finishing a real sign-in with a real account (that needs a human to sign in).

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated

## Review

- Codex and independent Opus reviews ran several rounds. The final Codex review on the head found no issues. Fixed from their findings:
  - each flow is pinned to the pairing it started on
  - a cancel the login refused (it had already signed in) now reports the added account
  - Claude's stdin can no longer crash the server with EPIPE
  - only the provider's own sign-in hosts are accepted, on both sides
  - pasted codes may not contain spaces
  - a sign-in stopped by an account change on the server says so
  - Codex cancels its own login, not whichever login is current
  - Claude's link is read from stdout only
  - after review round 3, the client was rebuilt as one explicit state machine per server and provider (checking → starting → following → settled). A Cancel is a flag that the loop delivers once the server names its flow, and asks again until the server takes it. A second Add joins the running sign-in. The server sign-in's Cancel sits in its own prompt, so it always targets that server, and it reappears if Settings is reopened mid-sign-in. The header Cancel stops whichever login that Add started, even after the host picker moves. Only lost answers are retried, and only within the server's 90-second window.
- Design check: this follows the usual shape for remote sign-in. The process and the tokens stay on the machine that uses them. Sign-in flows that call back to localhost (which would land on the wrong machine) are not offered. The client only opens the page and shows or relays a code. The approach did not change; only the client bookkeeping was simplified.
- The local orcad terminal smoke fails on this Mac at the file-watcher step, an environment problem unrelated to accounts, so CI covers it. The Node 18 process-host smoke needs a Node 18 runtime, and this package is unchanged. Every other step of the static job passes locally.
- Known follow-ups:
  - Cancel does not abort a long-poll Wait already in flight. The cancel reaches the server right away, so the only cost is waiting up to 20 seconds for that poll to return.
  - A re-pair during a sign-in is refused by the pairing pin rather than joined.
  - In one edge case (a local Add running while Settings shows a server that still has an earlier sign-in from before Settings reopened), two Cancel buttons appear with the same label. The header one stops the local login and the prompt one stops the server's. Both are correct, but the labels don't say which is which.
  - The header Cancel reads which login it should stop without subscribing to changes. It is only read while an add is running, and the pane re-renders whenever that changes, so the value is not stale in practice.
  - This client runs one server sign-in per provider at a time. A second server is told to finish or cancel the first.
  - Re-authenticating an existing account from a remote client, Windows servers, and WSL-distro account locations on a remote server are not covered yet.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable

## Notes

- Security: the server only publishes `https` links to the provider's sign-in hosts, and the client opens only `https` links. Pasted codes are never logged. Error text has terminal escape codes removed and is capped at 600 characters.
- SSH/remote: everything runs on the server that owns the accounts. Mixed versions are covered by the capability check. Mobile is unchanged.

- [x] I explained what changed and why
- [ ] Before/after screenshots: not attached (see above)
- [x] Self-reviewed for correctness, security, and performance

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

When your laptop sleeps and the SSH connection comes back, Orca repaints each terminal from a picture of the screen that the remote host keeps. Sometimes the host can't send that picture. When that happened, a full-screen program that was sitting idle (Claude Code, Codex, vim, and so on) kept showing the screen from before the disconnect, because it only redraws the parts that change. Now, when no picture arrives, Orca asks the program itself to redraw.

## What Changed

**Before:** after a reconnect where the host could not send a screen image, the pane printed "Orca skipped hidden terminal output…" and then stayed on the old frame. For example, a spinner and timer stayed frozen even though the agent had finished its turn. `orca terminal read --screen` from the desktop showed the same old frame, because it reads what the pane holds. Resizing the pane by hand was the only way to fix it.

**After:** the pane redraws on its own within about half a second of finding out the host has no image.

**Mechanism:** a remote pane now has one function that asks the program to repaint (`remote-program-redraw.ts`). It is called from every place that ends without a host image:
- the "restore unavailable" notice. It covers images that are too large for the replay limit, a host with no buffer, overflowed output, and requests that are never answered.
- the "could not restore history" notice after a parked pane is revealed.
- a snapshot reply that carries no image.

The redraw works like this. The pane makes the terminal one row shorter, or one row taller if it is already at the host's minimum height. It waits until the host confirms the new size, then puts the size back 250 ms later. Programs built on Node, such as Claude Code, ignore a resize signal when the size has not changed. That is why the redraw needs a real change, and why the two sizes have to arrive as separate events. Once the host's confirmation is in, both of those hold.

It does not touch the size when:
- the pane is hidden,
- the stream is still reconnecting,
- a phone or another desktop holds the terminal's size.

If another viewer takes the size during the redraw, the pane does not take it back. It always puts back the row it changed, even if the pane closes partway through.

## Why

The screen image from the host is still the main way a pane catches up. This change only covers the cases where that image cannot be had. Some alternatives I considered:

- **A same-size resize signal.** Node-based programs ignore it, so Claude Code would not redraw.
- **Retrying a smaller, screen-only snapshot.** This helps only the "too large" case. It does nothing for a host that has no buffer, or one that never answers.
- **A new "redraw" command on the host.** Older hosts would not have it, and both client and host would have to support it before it could be used. A one-row resize uses frames that every host already understands.

Before settling on this, I checked how terminal multiplexers force a repaint. They also apply two separate resizes, spaced apart in time, because a resize that ends at the starting size is otherwise merged away. Waiting for the host's confirmation follows the same rule, so the approach stayed as it was.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #26887

Thanks to the reporter for the detailed timeline and the resize workaround that pointed straight at this, and to @Tamaz-sujashvili.

## Visual Proof

No new UI. The end-to-end spec below covers the behavior: it fails on `main` with the pane still showing `FRAME:BEFORE` and the loss notice, while the program on the host has already drawn `FRAME:AFTER`. It passes with this change.

## Testing

- `remote-reconnect-unimaged-pane-redraw.test.ts` (new) drives a reconnected remote pane through every way the image can be missing. That covers images that are too large, a host with no buffer, overflowed output, requests that are never answered, the alternate screen, hidden then revealed, a phone holding the size, the minimum height, put-back only after the host confirms, a viewer taking the size during the redraw, and closing the pane during the redraw. A control case, where the host image arrives, checks that nothing is resized. 7 of these cases failed on `main` before the fix.
- `park-reveal-snapshot-verdict.test.ts` checks that the reveal notice asks for a redraw.
- `tests/e2e/paired-remote-terminal-reconnect-idle-frame.spec.ts` (new) uses two real Orca processes: a paired host and a desktop client. A full-screen program runs behind a TCP proxy. The proxy cuts the connection, the program changes its frame and goes idle, and then the connection comes back. It runs in two ways:
  - Host with a screen image: passes on `main` and with this change.
  - Host forced to have no image: **fails on `main`, passes with this change.** The spec checks that the program itself redrew.
- `tests/e2e/ssh-orcad-terminal-reconnect-idle-frame.spec.ts` (new) runs the same scenario over real SSH against a managed Orca server in Docker, so CI covers it.
- `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane` (553 files) and `src/main/runtime/rpc/methods/terminal` pass with one worker. The full static analysis and typecheck job passes locally.
- **Verified live:** on macOS, the paired host/client end-to-end test with a real connection cut, run against both `main` and this branch.
- **Covered only by CI:** the Docker managed-SSH lane, because Docker was not available on my machine. Not tested on Windows or Linux desktops.

## Notes

- **Remote compatibility:** uses only viewport frames that hosts already accept. Older hosts that never confirm a size get the row back after 2 s.
- **Host change:** only an end-to-end test hook. When a host is forced to have no image, it also skips its text-tail fallback.
- **Mobile:** if a phone holds the size, the pane never resizes the terminal.
- **Shell panes:** the redraw also happens on a plain shell pane that lost its image. Some shells reprint their prompt when the size changes, so the pane may show one extra prompt line. That is harmless, and it happens only when the host image was already lost.
- **Cross-platform:** the change is in the renderer only, with no platform-specific code.

selected_prs.title: feat(acp-chat): sidebar parity, background work menu and subagents for ACP chat
selected_prs.body: ## Summary ACP chat agents (`acp-chat` flag) now behave like terminal agents everywhere outside the pane, and the background work they start is visible and stoppable in one place. 1. **Sidebar and workspace parity**: status dots, chime, agent count, ports, workspace auto-naming, last-active ranking and page-comment delivery work for a pane on the chat surface. 2. **Standardised background work**: dev servers and subagents are reported through the JetBrains AIR ACP extension that claude-agent-acp and codex-acp both speak, as one `backgroundTasks` list on the chat session. 3. **Workspace activity menu**: the Pages menu moves to the tab bar and groups background processes (with stop), subagents and pages. It replaces the background terminals button. **Also includes:** a queued-prompt badge on sidebar rows, the chat session title as the pane title, scroll-to-load for older messages, tool runs that collapse once the turn moves on, and composer buttons sized to match. --- ## Part 1: Sidebar and workspace parity ### Why Switching an agent pane to the chat surface kills its pty, which ends the terminal agent binding. Every sidebar signal is keyed by that binding, so a chat showed no status, count, ports or title, and a workspace opened straight into a chat stayed "New workspace". ### How - A `LiveSessionObserver` in chat-runtime lets the host follow sessions. `chat-v3/chatAgentBridge.ts` reports each chat under the pane's terminal id, which the renderer now passes as an optional `terminalId` on `createSession`. - Chat bindings live in memory in `TerminalAgentStore` and merge into `listByWorkspace`. The lifecycle fan-out (broadcast, activity, naming, linked-task start) is shared with the hook handler via `fan-out-agent-lifecycle.ts`. - The adapter pid is registered with the port scanner, and `SUPERSET_TERMINAL_ID` is set in the agent env, so detached dev servers are attributed. The reaper leaves chat-owned port sessions alone. - Page watches deliver to the chat as a prompt (`promptChatSession`). That only happens when a chat is attached to the terminal, which only happens behind the flag. Otherwise delivery is unchanged. - `workspaces.create` and `createSession` take an optional `namingAgent`, so chat-opened workspaces get an AI title. ## Part 2: Background tasks and subagents ### Why Users could not see that an agent had a dev server running or a subagent working, and could not stop either. ### How - The adapter advertises AIR `asyncTasks` and `nativeSubagentSessions`. It folds `async_task_*`, `subagent_spawned/state_update` and ACP v2 `subagent_update` into a shared `BackgroundTasks` tracker. - Child-session output stays out of the parent transcript. A subagent gets one transcript row, and its latest step becomes its detail, coalesced to one update a second. - `stopBackgroundTask` runs protocol → router → live session → adapter (`_session/async_task/stop`). | Decision | Choice | Rationale | |---|---|---| | Source of truth | AIR extension, not `_meta.claudeCode` | Both shipped ACP adapters implement it, so any AIR-speaking agent works without UI changes | | Surface | Workspace-level menu, not a strip on the composer | Covers every agent in the workspace and keeps the composer clean | | Stop all | Agent tasks only | Detached terminals keep a per-row stop; one click should not kill a user's dev servers | ## Part 3: Desktop - `WorkspaceActivityMenu` (renamed from `WorkspacePagesMenu`): groups with a header action, and a running-count dot on the trigger. - `BackgroundTerminalsButton` is removed. Its helpers moved to `$workspaceId/utils/backgroundTerminals`. - `DashboardSidebarWorkspaceQueuedBadge`: queued prompt count per workspace. - `useLoadOlderOnReach` replaces the "Load earlier messages" button. - `transcriptRows`: a tool run collapses once later entries exist and none of its tools are running. --- ## Manual QA Checked in the dev app over CDP with the `acp-chat` and `chat-v3` flag overrides: - [x] Chat-opened workspace gets an AI title in the sidebar ("Add port conflict troubleshooting to README") - [x] Activity menu lists a chat's background dev server with stop and stop-all; Pages group has "+", no "View all" - [x] Sidebar row shows the working state and the port chip for a chat agent - [x] Header button height matches Changes/Commit (28px); composer Send matches the pickers (26px) - [x] Live probe against claude-agent-acp 0.85: a background shell task and a native subagent appear, show their step, and clear when done; subagent tool calls stay out of the parent transcript Not verified end to end: - [ ] Page comment delivered into a chat - [ ] Queued badge with a busy chat - [ ] Stopping a task from the menu - [ ] codex-acp ## Testing - `bun test` in `packages/chat` (42), `packages/chat-runtime` (193), host-service chat-v3, terminal-agents, page-watch, notifications and terminal-agents router (264), and the desktop v2-workspace and DashboardSidebar suites (631). All pass. - `tsc --noEmit` is clean for every touched file. The remaining errors in this worktree are ungenerated route types and auth typings on main. - `bun run check:i18n` passes, with all new strings translated in 16 locales. - The full host-service suite has 41 failures in git-watcher, tunnel dial and git-helpers tests that this branch does not touch (`jest.advanceTimersByTime` is missing under the local Bun 1.3.2). ## What changes for users without the flag The activity menu ships to everyone, because it replaces the Pages menu and the background terminals button: - The trigger is always in the tab bar. It shows a running dot and count for agent background tasks and subagents (terminal agents' subagents included); idle detached terminals are listed but not counted. - Detached terminals keep a per-row stop and reopen on click. The attach debounce and a loading state carry over from the old button, and terminals shown in the right pane area (#8194) count as attached. - Pages moved here from the right sidebar and right pane area headers. - Terminal-agent subagents now appear in the Subagents group; clicking one opens its transcript. ## Compatibility All tRPC changes are additive and optional (`terminalId`, `namingAgent`, `stopBackgroundTask`, binding fields `chatSessionId`, `backgroundTasks`, `queuedPrompts`). Older hosts strip the unknown inputs and never emit the new fields, so the new UI stays empty. ## Known Limitations - Only AIR-speaking ACP adapters report background work. The native (non-ACP) Claude and Codex harnesses don't feed the tracker yet. - Chat subagents are not in the sidebar agents chip, because its rows open a transcript file that only terminal agents have. - A page watch registered while the pane was a terminal is dropped when the pane switches to chat. Publishing again from the chat re-registers it. - Chat bindings are in memory; after a host restart they return when the pane re-creates its session. ## Follow-ups - `agents run --continue` on a chat pane should prompt the chat instead of launching a terminal agent. ## Rollout / Rollback Behind the existing `acp-chat` flag. With the flag off, no chat sessions exist and every terminal path is unchanged. The exception is the activity menu replacing the background terminals button, which ships to everyone. Rollback is a revert of the three commits. --- ## Summary by cubic ACP chat agents behind the `acp-chat` flag now behave like terminal agents everywhere outside the pane, and the background work they start — dev servers and subagents — is visible and stoppable from a new workspace activity menu. **Background work** - Chat sessions report under the pane's terminal id, so sidebar status, ports, agent count, workspace naming, and page-comment delivery work as with terminal agents. - Dev servers and subagents come from the JetBrains AIR extension that claude-agent-acp and codex-acp both speak, folded into one `backgroundTasks` list; subagent output stays out of the parent transcript, and stale or duplicate updates don't revive a finished subagent. Once the parent session is known, updates from any other session — including those arriving while a resume replays history — are treated as child activity, so a stray titled tool call never reaches the parent transcript. - Step changes travel as live-only `background` deltas, so they don't journal or bump the session's `updatedAt`; the task list itself stays durable. - `stopBackgroundTask` stops a chat's background task from the menu — only tasks the adapter knows and can stop — and detached terminals keep their per-row stop. A disconnected subagent shows as failed, and clearing a dead chat's statuses leaves it failed so it isn't treated as alive. - Chat bindings live in memory and reappear when the pane re-creates its session after a host restart; closing a fork only falls back to the original chat when the replacement never started, and a pane that adopts a branched copy closes the chat it branched from. **UI** - Pages and background work move into the tab bar's workspace activity menu, which replaces the background terminals button and ships to everyone; the menu debounces pane attachment, shows a loading state for terminal sessions, its running dot counts agent tasks and subagents rather than idle detached terminals, its clock follows every listed row, and arrow keys move between items. - Sidebar rows show a queued-prompt badge (announced to screen readers); chat panes take the session title; resumed chats open at their end only after the session starts; older messages load on scroll once the user has scrolled up, with a retry on failure; tool runs collapse once the turn moves past them; composer buttons match the pickers. Written for commit cd70fd3b0e821602bbd41344c498b8391f15bdfb. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added a workspace activity menu that brings background processes, subagents, workspace pages, and pinned pages together. Open or stop eligible background work, stop all stoppable agent tasks, and create pages from the menu. * Workspace items display queued-message counts. * Chat transcripts load older messages as you scroll, with progress and retry feedback. * Supported background tasks can be stopped, and chat sessions can display updated titles. * Workspace naming can use the selected agent when creating a chat workspace. * **Bug Fixes** * Improved tool-call collapsing while keeping active work and pending approvals visible. * Chat transcripts show a loading state while a session is starting, even when messages are already present.

selected_prs.title: feat(chat): steer prompts into a running ACP turn, hide stop while only background work runs
selected_prs.body:
## What & why

In ACP chat, a message sent while background subagents were running went into the queue and waited until they finished. The main agent was idle the whole time, so you couldn't talk to it.

The cause: `@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp` keeps `session/prompt` open while subagents it spawned are still running (`Turn.deferredSettle`). The runtime saw a running turn and queued every follow-up. The composer also kept showing stop. Pressing it sent `session/cancel`, and Claude's adapter then cancels every background subagent (`nativeSubagentRuntime.finishAll("cancelled")`).

**Steering into the running turn**
- Claude's and Codex's ACP adapters support the `_session/steering` extension and advertise it as `initialize._meta.steering.supported`.
- **Adapter** (`acpAdapter.ts`): `steer()` sends `_session/steering` with `idleBehavior: "promptRequired"`. Claude then hands the message back if no turn is running.
- **When it steers:**
  - Plain Enter steers only while the turn is waiting on background work (see below). Otherwise it queues, as before. Claude steers at priority `now`, so steering every Enter would cut off the reply in progress.
  - Cmd+Enter, and Steer on a queued prompt, steer at any time. They use `_session/steering` instead of cancelling the turn.
  - When a turn becomes background-only, prompts queued while the agent was working go into it in order. They are restamped so the transcript shows them where they were delivered.
- **Order:** steers run one at a time, in send order. Pending steers count as busy, so a prompt sent later can't overtake one.
- **Fallback:** if the agent doesn't accept the message, if the queue is paused, or if a different turn is running by then, the message goes back to the queue. It goes ahead of prompts sent after it. A queued prompt you chose to steer stays first and interrupts the turn, as before.
- **Turn check:** a prompt that names a turn that is no longer running is queued.
- **Stop:** stop with pause also pauses steers still pending.
- **Session end:** a steer still pending when the session stops is discarded.
- **Other agents:** pi, OpenCode (checked 1.15.5) and Gemini don't advertise steering, so they keep today's queue.

**No stop button while only background work runs**
- **Signal:** the ACP adapter reports `awaitingBackground` on session state. It is true when the agent supports steering, the turn is still open, the agent's last model cycle has ended, and background tasks are live. Claude sends `usage_update` with `cost` at each result, so that marks the cycle end.
- **Composer:** while `awaitingBackground` is true it shows send instead of stop. Stopping background work stays in the background-tasks menu at the top.
- **Protocol:** `awaitingBackground` is a new optional field. Older clients ignore it, and newer clients against an older host see it missing and show stop as before.

**Known limit (Codex):** Codex has no `promptRequired` option. If its turn ends just as a steer arrives, Codex starts a new turn itself and answers `startedNewTurn`. codex-acp never tells the client when that turn ends (`turn/completed` stays inside the adapter), so the runtime can't track it. Status can read idle while Codex answers. The window is the moment between Codex finishing its turn and our `session/prompt` response. Codex never reports `awaitingBackground`, so only an explicit Steer can hit it. The real fix is upstream: codex-acp should honor `promptRequired`, which our adapter already sends.

## How I tested it

- **Unit tests:** `packages/chat-runtime` (223) and `packages/chat` (42) pass, and typecheck passes for both. Repo-wide `bun run lint` is clean. There is a regression test for each review finding. The ones for "plain Enter queues while working", "later prompt can't overtake", and "pause stops an undispatched steer" fail on the previous commit.
- **Real agents, through the runtime with a script:**
  - **Claude:** a message sent while Claude was working queued. Once the turn was background-only, it went in and Claude answered it. A later message went straight in and was answered in about 2 s while the subagent was still running. `awaitingBackground` turned on during the hold and off while each answer streamed.
  - **Claude baseline (main):** the follow-up queued and was answered about 77 s later, after the subagent finished.
  - **Codex** (`gpt-5.5`): a steered message joined the running turn. The tool row ends `completed` with and without steering.
- **Dev app over CDP** (this branch, local stack, Local Admin, Claude chat):
  - While Claude was working, an early follow-up queued, with Steer and delete controls and the stop button.
  - Once the turn was background-only, it went in and was answered, in the right order. The composer showed send and the top indicator showed 1 background task.
  - "17 + 25" went straight in: stop at 2.6 s, "42" at 2.8 s, back to send at 3.5 s.
  - The turn closed normally when the subagent finished.
- **Local typecheck of `desktop`, `host-service` and `mobile`** fails only on better-auth types in `packages/auth` and `packages/trpc`, which this PR doesn't touch. Two copies of `@better-auth/core` resolved in this checkout. CI Typecheck passes.

## Checklist

- [x] PR title follows conventional commits (`type(scope): subject`)
- [x] `bun run lint` passes. Typecheck passes for the changed packages; see the note above for desktop, host-service and mobile locally.
- [ ] "Allow edits from maintainers" is checked on fork PRs

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Prompts can be sent directly to an eligible running turn when steering is supported, including while it waits on background work; prompts that cannot be accepted remain queued.
  * Sessions indicate when a turn has finished its current cycle and is waiting for background work.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Turn cancellation is unavailable while background work is pending.
  * Queued prompts retain their order when steering is declined, canceled, or unavailable.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

selected_prs.title: feat(desktop,host-service): show Hermes token usage in the usage section
selected_prs.body: ## Summary - Hermes Agent token usage now appears in Settings → Usage, with its own line in the chart and its own cost estimate. - New host-service reader for Hermes's `state.db`, registered beside the Devin and OpenCode SQLite readers. ## Why / Context `types.ts` listed Hermes as an agent that "records no usable local usage data". That is no longer true: Hermes writes token counts to `/state.db` (schema v26 as of this PR): - `sessions` — per-session totals (input, output, cache read/write, reasoning), cost, model, cwd, title. - `session_model_usage` — the same totals split per model and per task (the main loop, plus side calls like title generation and compression). ## How It Works - `history/hermes.ts` opens each `state.db` read-only and selects sessions active since the cutoff, plus their per-model rows. Homes: `~/.hermes` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on Windows), every `profiles/` under it, and `HERMES_HOME`. - `history/hermes-rows.ts` (pure, unit-tested) copies the accounting of `hermes insights`: one entry per per-model row, plus the part of each session total that no per-model row covers. Without that second step we would undercount older sessions and gateway runs, which only write session totals. - Hermes `input_tokens` already excludes cache reads/writes, so it maps directly to `uncachedInput`. Reasoning is a subset of output, as with Codex. - When Hermes records a cost, it is used as `costUsd`. Otherwise the shared multi-model price table applies. - Desktop: `hermes` is added to `AGENT_CHART_CONFIG` / `AGENT_ICON_KEY` / `AGENT_ORDER` with bronze `#8c5c14`. That color has the best separation from the other 12 hues I could find at the palette's chroma: ≥ 13.3 ΔE under normal vision, 9.3 CVD ΔE from Devin next to it, and lightness band, chroma and 3:1 contrast pass in light and dark. ## Manual QA Checklist - [x] Reader run in Node (under the desktop's Electron, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`) against a copy of a real Hermes `state.db` (schema v26) with one seeded session: per-model rows, the session remainder, and the session title came out as expected. - [x] A missing Hermes home returns 0 without throwing. - [x] Dev desktop over CDP (real clicks), with two real `hermes chat -q` sessions: the legend, tooltip and totals matched `state.db` ($0.15 / 40K after one session; $0.19 / 73K after two, 7d view). ## Testing - `bun test src/trpc/router/usage` in `packages/host-service`: 142 pass. This includes the new `hermes-rows.test.ts`, which I confirmed fails when the remainder subtraction is broken. - `bunx biome check` on the changed files: clean. - `turbo run typecheck` for host-service and desktop: no errors in changed files. Both fail locally on better-auth plugin types in `packages/auth` / `packages/trpc`, because this worktree's `node_modules` is older than its lockfile. CI will be the real check. ## Known Limitations - Hermes sums tokens per session and model, not per day. A session that runs over several days is counted on the day it was last active. - Like `hermes insights`, the remainder is computed per field and clamped at 0. If side-call rows exceed the main-loop session total in one field, a real legacy remainder in that field can be hidden. ## Compatibility - `UsageAgent` gains `"hermes"`. The leaderboard upload sends it as `provider`, which the API validates as `z.string()`, so released API builds accept it. - Released desktops (≤ 1.37) read `AGENT_CHART_CONFIG[row.agent].color` unguarded in the model table. A released desktop viewing a newer **remote** host's Usage (`?workspaceId=`), where a Hermes model ranks in the top 6 by cost, will crash that page. The local host ships with the desktop, so it is not affected. This PR adds `?.` so desktops from this release on tolerate agents they don't know. Devin and Muse had the same exposure when they were added. --- ## Summary by cubic Shows Hermes Agent token usage in Settings → Usage by reading token counts from `/state.db` during host-service collection. Hermes appears in the usage chart with its own line, cost estimate, and a bronze color. - Adds the new host-service reader beside the Devin and OpenCode SQLite readers, scanning the default home, every profile under it, and `HERMES_HOME` (real-pathed and deduped so symlinks or trailing slashes don't double-count). - Replicates `hermes insights` accounting: one entry per per-model row, plus the part of each session total no row covers, so older sessions and gateway runs aren't undercounted. Reads sessions and per-model rows in one transaction. - Maps Hermes `input_tokens` directly to `uncachedInput` since it already excludes cache reads and writes. - Uses Hermes-recorded cost when present; otherwise falls back to the shared multi-model price table. - `UsageAgent` gains `"hermes"`, and the leaderboard upload sends it as `provider`, which the API validates as a string, so released API builds accept it. - The Usage model table now guards its agent color lookup so a host that reports an unknown agent can't crash the page. Written for commit 165b82d7193dcc0e1a14180743302075311026dc. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added Hermes usage history to the usage dashboard, including session labels, token totals, and cost reporting when available. * Hermes activity is included in the agent chart and legend.

selected_prs.title: feat(desktop): set up a host over SSH from Settings → Hosts
selected_prs.body: **Links** - Plan: `plans/20261010-add-host-over-ssh.md` (phase 2). Builds on #8386 (API) and #8388 (`superset hosts add`). ## Summary - Settings → Hosts gets a **Set up a host over SSH** row at the top of the host list. - It opens a dialog that asks for the SSH destination and runs `superset hosts add ` in an embedded terminal. Passwords, MFA, host-key questions and the install prompt work as in any terminal, with no new UI for each. ## How it works - **Terminal:** the dialog reuses `CommandTerminal`, the workspace-free terminal the GitHub sign-in dialog uses. The phases are form, running, success (exit 0) and failed (Retry, with an editable target). The dialog can't be dismissed while the command runs. On success it invalidates `host.roster`, so the new host appears in the list. - **Auth:** the command sets `SUPERSET_ORGANIZATION_ID`. These terminals already set `SUPERSET_WORKSPACE_ID`, so the bundled CLI takes the app account's token from the local host (`host.apiToken`, #8274), as it does in a workspace terminal. No second login is needed and no token appears in argv. With no local host, or an older one without `host.apiToken`, it runs `superset auth login` first. - **Safety:** the target is shell-quoted and must not contain spaces or start with `-`. The CLI now refuses a leading `-` too, so ssh can never read the target as an option (`-oProxyCommand=…`). ## Manual QA (dev app over CDP, port 9555, renderer on this worktree's 6965) - [x] The sidebar row opens the dialog with focus in the input. "Set up" is disabled when the input is empty and for `-oProxyCommand=evil`. - [x] End to end against a Docker Ubuntu box with systemd (`ssh://dev@127.0.0.1:2233`). The dev shim was pointed at a production CLI build for this run, because the box talks to production: - the host-key question was answered in the embedded terminal; - the password prompt worked; a first try failed on timing, which showed the **failed** state (warning line, output kept, Retry), and Retry then succeeded; - the output showed signed in, systemd user service started, online, and the gh warning; - the dialog then showed "The host is online…" with Done. - [x] Host-token auth with no CLI login: against the dev host, `auth whoami` reports `authSource: host`, and `apiKey.create` with that token mints a key (revoked afterwards). - [ ] The new host appearing in the sidebar: not seen in dev, whose roster is the dev database while the box registered in production. The roster invalidation runs on exit 0. ### After review fixes (912cf3b) - [x] Escape and ✕ cannot close the dialog during setup. Checked over CDP: Escape mid-run, the dialog stays open and no close button is rendered; the ✕ returns when setup finishes. - [x] Empty-state button removed. Its dialog lived inside the "no hosts" branch and unmounted when the first host appeared. The sidebar row sits in the hosts layout, which stays mounted. - [x] The description now says "signs Superset in to your account", retranslated in all 16 locales. - Filmed end to end over CDP, with the frames on the feature page: https://app.superset.sh/page/scripts-can-now-wait-on-agents-press-keys-attach-a-158c55 (section 5). ### UX pass (256abe3), every path driven over CDP with real mouse and keyboard input | Path | Result | |---|---| | Cancel during setup | Returns to the form and ends `hosts add` and ssh. This found a bug: React reused the Cancel element as the submit button, so a click restarted setup. Fixed. | | Focus | The terminal has focus when setup starts; the host-key `yes` was typed with no click. A status line says to answer prompts there. | | Agent key | Logged in with no password (dev needed `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` passed through turbo; packaged apps get it from launchd, checked on Canary). | | Unknown name / refused port / wrong password ×3 / password after 130 s | Each shows ssh's own line plus a matching hint. The 130 s case is sshd's 120 s `LoginGraceTime`, which it closes without logging. | | Fresh box (no CLI, lingering off, sudo asks for a password) | Install consent prompt → installer ran → after Retry: lingering prompt → `sudo` password → online, `Linger=yes`, service active. | | No CLI login and no host manifest | `superset auth login` appears inside the dialog; Cancel stops it. | | Success | "Open host" replaces Set up and opens the new host's page. | | Wrapping | CLI messages, yes/no questions and error hints wrap at word boundaries. | ### Final end-to-end run on a0555330 (after cleanup) - **CLI** against the Docker Ubuntu box, production API: `hosts add` → signed in, systemd service started, online. A re-run reports "Already signed in" and "service unchanged". `hosts remove` → service gone, no host processes, key revoked. - **Dialog over CDP** (dev app, real mouse and keyboard): - host-key question answered with no click (the terminal had focus); - agent-key login, online, then "Open host" opened `/settings/hosts/`; - Cancel at the password prompt returned to the form and left no setup process; - a refused port showed its hint. - **Cleanup:** the dialog quotes its command with the existing `quoteShellToken` instead of a private copy; restating comments removed; the systemd and launchd names are no longer exported. ## Testing - `bun test` for `buildHostsAddCommand`: quoting, and refusing option-like targets. - `bun run check:i18n`: the six new strings are translated in all 16 locales. - `bun run lint`. Desktop typecheck shows only the existing better-auth type errors (`onboardedAt` and similar); none in the changed files. ## Known limitations - Hosts running a desktop build without `host.apiToken` (before #8274) fall back to `superset auth login` in the dialog. - Docs for the whole SSH set (CLI reference and the docs site) come in a follow-up, now that every piece is in. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds the ability to set up a new host over SSH from Settings → Hosts. A new row at the top of the host list opens a dialog that runs `superset hosts add ` in an embedded terminal, so password, MFA, and host-key prompts behave exactly as they would in a terminal. **Setup flow** - The dialog has form, running, success, and failed states; on success it refetches the host roster so the new host appears. - The command sets `SUPERSET_ORGANIZATION_ID` and signs in through the local host's API token, so no re-login is needed; without a local host, it runs `superset auth login` first. - The terminal gets focus when setup starts, and Open host replaces Set up on success. Open host reads the new host's id from the command's output, whether the "(id) is online" line or the JSON result for agent environments that print neither. - The dialog can't be dismissed while setup runs; Cancel ends the session and returns to the form. **Safety** - The destination must not contain spaces or start with `-`, and the CLI now rejects leading-dash targets so ssh can't interpret the input as an option. - The target is shell-quoted before being passed to the command. - ssh failures now explain the cause (wrong password, changed host key, slow answer, unreachable port); the changed host-key hint points at the `ssh-keygen -R` command ssh already printed. CLI messages and errors wrap at word boundaries on narrow terminals. Written for commit 1f88109772bf88d2fe33de3f82754b1c1b3d1b9e. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Set up a host over SSH from Hosts settings. Enter an SSH destination to install and run Superset on a remote machine; follow setup progress and errors in the dialog, retry failed setup, or open the host when it’s ready. - Once online, the host can be selected when creating a workspace. - **Bug Fixes** - SSH destinations beginning with a dash are rejected to prevent invalid connection targets. - SSH connection failures now include more specific troubleshooting guidance, and long terminal messages are easier to read.
